We insert this afternoon for the perusal of our readers the following translation þÿ the original of which is contained in the Gaceta dc Gobitrno, ot Santo Domingo, dated 11th instant þÿ ol the articles of a Treaty to he concluded between our Government and that of the Dominican Republic : þÿ "His Majesty the King of Denmark, and the President of the Dominican Republic, animated with the desire to rela- litate and extend the commercial facitions in operation long before this, between both countries, have resolved to conclude a Treaty of Amity, Commerce and Navigation, having tor its basis the principles of the most perfect reciprocity. With this object they have appointed their respective Plenipotentiaries, namely : His Majesty the King of Denmark þÿ Hans Ditinar Frederick Feddersen, Knight of the Order of Dannebrog, and Governor of his West India Colonies; ami the President of the Dominican Republic charged with the Executive power þÿ nipotentiary Segisniundo Rothschild, Special after fortius purpose, who, Plehaving exchanged their lull powers, and having found the same complete and fol- in proper form, have agreed upon the lowing Articles : Art. 1. þÿ There shall he peace and perpetual amity between His Majesty the King of Denmark, his heirs or successors, and the Dominican Republic, and t lie subjects and citizens of both conntries. Art. 2. þÿ The subjects of His Majesty the King of Denmark shall enjoy in ail the cities or provinces of the Dominican

Republic, and the citizens of this Republic in all ports or provinces of Denmark, an equal right or privilege as already granted, or which may in future he granted to the subjects or citizens ol the most favored nation. The subjects of His Danish Majesty will he able to reside, trade or traffic in all parts of the territories of the Republic, in which are admitted at this moment, or may be henceforth admitted, the subjects or citizens of the most favored nation, and will enjoy the most perfect protection in regard to their person or property. In the same manner the citizens of the Dominican Republic will be able to reside, trade or traffic, in all parts of the territory of Denmark, through its extent where strangers are received or admitted as subjects of the most favored nation, and will enjoy the most perfect protection in regard to their person or property.

Ait. 3. þÿ The Danish vessels in the ports of the Dominican Republic, and ail the merchandize, or articles ol ccn.meico imported or exported in said vessels, in no case cart be subject on their arrival or departure to any other or higher Ous tone-House charges or imposts in regard to duties or tonnage than those which are levied upon the National vessels or subjects, or the articles of commerce imported or exported by the said National vessels. And in a similar manner the Dominican vessels, in the ports of Denmark, and all the merchandize, or articles of commerce which are imported or exported by the said Dominican vessels, in no case can he subject, on their arrival or departure to any other or higher Customllouse charges or imposts in regard to duties or tonnage, than those which are levied upon the Danish vessels or subjects, or the articles of commerce imported or exported Danish vessels. by The Dominican vessels will be admitted in the colonies of His Majesty the King of Denmark, comprising the Islands ofFaeroe, Iceland and Gronland, under the same conditions as are, or will be admitted in future the merchant vessels of the most favored nation. Art. 4. þÿ The coasting trade is not to be practised in the respective states of the contracting parties, by the vessels of each party, unless subsequently permitted to do so by the laws of each state; but. it remains determined that the citizens of either party are to enjoy all the rights granted, or which may be granted,

regarding this matter to the most favoieil nation. Art. 5. þÿ The importation by vessels of either nation, of all staple products or industry, as well as manufactures and articles of commerce, whatever may be their classification, known as proceeding from the Danish dominions or any other possessions brought in Danish vessels, cannot be prohibited, nor can the said products, merchandize, or articles ol commerce, belonging to whatever country, and imported in Dominican vessels, be subject to any other or greater duties than those which are imposed on the most favored nation. In regard to the exportation of all kind of produce of the Dominican Republic, Danish subjects or vessels will enjoy the same rights and privileges which are or would be accorded to any other favored nation. Aif (5. þÿ The Dominican Republic hinds itself to afford to vessels under the Danish flag, their officers and crew, the protection which they may require. In cases of shipwreck or distress of any Danish vessels on the coast of the Republic, the local authorities are under the obligation to afford all the assistance necessary, either as to the safety of the crew and cargo, or towards the recovery of the wreck ; furthermore with regard to the duties or charges for salvage, or of the recovery of the vessel and cargo, all matters appertaining thereto will be treated or dealt with in the same manner as if connected with any National vessel under similar circumstances. When from cases of distress or damage

and tor the object of preserving the cargo of the vessel, one of the contracting other, the parties may put vessel said into the harbour of the will not be subject to any Custom-House or navigation charges, þÿ nation, whatever excepting may those be charges their denomi- which alone are allowed in cases of damage being the fees for pilotage or charges for services rendered by private individuals, þÿ provided these vessels do not practice any commercial operations, by either taking on board or discharging merchandize.

It will also be permitted to the said vessels to deposit on shore their cargoes to effect their repairs, without payingany duty, provided the said articles are reexported for account of the same proprietor, and in the same vessel, or in case the vessel has been condemned in any other vessel. Art. 7. þÿ Both nations having concluded to treat each other as the most favored, they formally pledge themselves in all matters relative to commerce and maritime interest to give immediate facilities as to the privileges or advantages, of whatsoever class which are or may be granted hereafter to other nations to Danish and Dominican subjects and citizens, and in their behalf gratuitous if the concession of the other nation has been gratuitous, or by virtue of a reasonable compensation if the concession is subject to any burthen. Art. 8. þÿ In the passage to the Sound and Belt the Dominican vessels and their cargoes will be treated according to the charges made against the most favored nation. Art. 9. þÿ Each of the contracting parties will have the right of appointing Consuls for the protection of tlieir commerce in the ports and cities of each others Dominions, but these Consulswill not enter on their executive functions ' without having previously obtained the exequator" of the government of the country in which they are to reside. The diplomatic Agents and respective Consuls will enjoy the same rights, privileges, immunities and exemptions which are accorded to the diplomatic Agents

and Cousuls of equal rank of the most favored nation. Art. 10. þÿ The vessels of war of each of the powers will enter, remain, and careen in each others ports, in which access is allowed to the vessels of the most favored nation, and will be subject to the same regulations, enjoying the same honor, privileges and exemptions. Art. II. þÿ The subjects of His Danish Majesty in the territory of the Dominican Republic cannot be disturbed, persecuted nor molested on the grounds of religion, hut to the contrary, they are to enjoy the most absolute liberty of conscience and it will be permitted them to exercise their religious functions in their dwellings, or particular chapels, or places ot worship. They also have the right ol interring in the cemeteries which they may establish and retain, the subjects ol His Danish Majesty who may die in the territory of the Dominican Republic ; and in the same manner the citizens ot the Dominican Republic will enjoy in all the Danish possessions the most absolute liberty of conscience, and will exercise their religious functions in their dwellings or particular places of worship destined for Divine Service. Art. 12. þÿ The vessels, cargoes, merchandize or effects belonging to the subjects and citizens of one or other of the two contracting parties, can never be subject to embargo, nor be retained for military expedition, nor any other use of whatever kind, without an indemnity, previously agreed upon with the parties concerned, and to a sufficient amount to

cover the injury, loss or delay, caused by the public service to which they may have been destined. Art. þÿ13. In case of any one of the two countries being at war with another power, nation or state, the citizens of the other will he at liberty to continue its commerce and intercourse with the same state, with the sole exception of the ports or places blockaded or besieged, but this liherty of trade or intercourse does not extend to articles which in time of war are considered contraband, 6uch as vannon, fire arms, warlike weapons, pro-

Art. 14. þÿ Will be considered as Danish in the harbours of the Republic, and as Dominicans in the Danish possessions, the vessels which bona fide belong to the citizens of the respective countries, and navigate under their respective flags, having on board the register and documents required by each of the states to establish their nationality and character as merchant vessels. St. Thomas Times, 28th April 1852. koll the st. thomas times. \ Hill tin" Compensation to the late Owners of Slaves in the Danish West India Possessions. I\ bringing to the notice of the public the fore-mentioned Hill, which on the Oth of February last was introduced in the Lower-House (Folkethinget) of the 1 Uigsdiig" of the Mother Cou try, we fee! ourselves constrained to make some remarks on the subject. Fain would we that an abler pen had undertaken the task, but "in the absence of a regular physician, a country practitioner may be allowed to prescribe." Whilst we give the Minister of Finance, Count tSponneck, his meed of praise, for the pains which he has taken in framing the l>ill, and the zeal be lias evinced on this and on former occasions in advocating the rights, and defending the interests of the colonists, we cannot but regret that expediency no doubt lias caused him to base the claim of the late slave owners on common justice and eajuity only ; for, as we shall prove in the following, their right is positively founded on strict justice and law. Nor are we less grieved that only a modicum of $40 per head is recommended to be given ; as it is certain that even one hundred dollars for each slave would not be an adequate payment for the loss sustained. As the Minister, however, has expressed bis views with candour and moderation, we reiterate our thanks for his noble efforts and labours in our just cause, and rest satisfied that he will light the good light with unabated zeal

and untlinching perseverance until justice is done to us, for the spoliation of our property. Hut notwithstanding the Government ras thus acknowledged that on the grounds of equity and justice we are entitled to compensation, and fixed the sum much lower that eitherGreat Hritain, France or Sweden has done in similar cases, yet there are some members of the " Folkething" who not only deny us indemnity, but strenuously oppose justice being done to us on that score. Painful as the fact is of itself, it becomes doubly poignant when we perceive such men as Messrs. David, Lehmann and Rot he among the number. Men whose sense of justice and equity we have always held, and, whatever inay be the result of the measure in question, will always hold as the most pre-eminent of their many other distinguished qualities. The saving institutions, established for such purposes, may be founded by private persons, societies or communities. As private undertakings they enjoy the advantage of being able to count upon greater protection in times of war, than if they were founded by the state. Government however must at all events examine and sanction their statutes and regulations, grant the permission of their establishment, inspect and superintend their management and administration as supreme guardian and, as such, examine the accounts, to be sent in annually. Simple savings banks, which receive the deposits of every participant and pay interest on them till they are paid back, and thus merely offer the advantage of such interest and the facility of depositing and withdrawing the smallest funds, are, according to the re-

sults of long and general experience, such beneficial institutions, that not too much zeal can be bestowed upon their extension and improvement. They serve in particular to nourish industry, diligence and temperance in the working classes, to heighten their confidence in their own powers and exertions, to secure a resource in cases of accident and misfortune, and thus, to obviate the necessity of assistance from any poor-fund, yes, they have often served, by dint of the collected capitals, to convert many a labourer into an independant producer and manufacturer. The bank stands under the control of the functionaries of the municipality, the funds of which will guarantee the safety of the deposited sums. c, By larger districts, so that all the communities, belonging to them, be combined, and the administration conducted by deputies from all of them. A compulsion to deposit money in the bank, can never be justified and is in itself hardly practicable, whilst on the other hand the ends of the institution may very safely be obtained without it, f. i., by trying to spread the knowledge of their advantages, to counteract and

The general rules for the establishment of such banks are : 1. It is advisable, to afford as frequent opportunities for depositing money as possible ; the bank ought to be open more than once a week, and several under-treasurers or receivers to be appointed in larger towns.

2. The bank must take the smallest amounts down to a certain minimum, fixed according to the local propositions of wages and revenues. Larger sums must not be received, as it cannot be the object of the institution, to facilitate the investment of capitals, which arc in the hands of people of fortune : this consideration will therefore lead to the fixation of a capital. 3. As the bank can render the sums, accumulated out oi a great number of small investments, productive of interest, it is thereby enabled to pay interest even on minor sums, which the owner would otherwise have no chance of applying to any immediate conducive purpose ; a measure, very and rational to encourage the industrious and saving depositor. The rate of interest will be fixed as high as the one for the lent sums and the cxpences of the institution will ever warrant, and it is but judicious, to make it understood in an easy and intelligible manner. I lie Hungarians have been relieved from a bitter unrelenting onemv ; and the despot of France cannot fail to miss a man who was ever ready to sanction any coup d'etat \\ hicli tended to crush the spirit of liberty. There existed a secret alliance between the French and the Austrian princes, the conditions of which were best known and understood by the Pope at Rome, and by the Jesuit party in Switzerland. The aggrandisement of the Roman Catholic C urrh. and the suppression of all popular rights, under the plea of curbing anarchical designs, were the secret common ties which hound the Austrian Minister and the Prince President of France to each other. Illustrated London Nats, 10 th April 1852. FRANCE. Louis Napoleon is fast advancing towards the completion of his most sanguine hopes. The Imperial throne is within view, and may he considered as attainable at the will of the Prince. The only matter of doubt appears to he as to the moment of fitting convenience when he may choose to assume the title of Emperor of the French; hut the thing itself seems settled, and he has obtained the grand desideratum which formed the ground of so much ill-will between him and the Legislative Assembly þÿ a large dotation. The first main act of the new Senate has been to vote M. Bonaparte 12,000,000 francs a year (£480,000), and to appropiate the national palaces, parks, gardens, furniture, &,c. to his use, togetlu r with the right of shooting and hunting in the national woods and forests of Versailles, Fontainebleau, Compiegne, Marly, and St. Germain. All the public bodies of the State have now taken the oath of allegiance to him ; and he has experienced the gratification ol receiving in due form what he so much desired and needed to consolidate his position, viz. the homage of the Church in the person of its leading dignitaries.

The " Prince President" of the French Republic has done so many surprising things in his time, that the public no longer feel astonishment at any of his acts or speeches, however marvellous they may be. Yet both Frenchmen and Englishmen, however blunted they may he against sudden impressions, will own to something like surprise at his last appearance before the pu.dic. He claims the throne þÿ for he scarcely conceals that such is his object þÿ not simply because he was elected President for four Years in 1848, and for ten years on the 1st of January, 1852, hut because, four vears before he was horn, the French people proclaimed by their voles that the future government of France should he hereditary in the family of Napoleon Bonaparte. Since the doctrine of Divine right has been exploded, and the dogma of the sovereignty of the people substituted for it, he claims, as he would have the world believe, to he a more legitimate ruler of the French than even the Count de Chamhord would be. He has gravelypropounded this doctrine to the judges of the superior courts ; and the Parisians, quite understanding what it means, have quietly made up their minds to witness within a few weeks the transformation of the President of ten years into the " hereditary Emperor of the French." It is asserted that the imperial robes are already made; that the soldiers are to have more sausages and more champagne on some early day in May ; and that all the rest will follow as a matter of course. As in his address to the Legislature,
upon which we commented last week,

To 0 Ifi 0 2 the President declared that he would not assume the crown of his uncle unless the conspiracies of factions forced him to do so, we may suppose that, for the sake of appearing consistent, a conspiracy will he ordered, as well as the robes and sausages, and that it will be as duly forthcoming whenever it is wanted. þÿ Ibid.

On Savings liSauks. (Concluded from our last.) 4. Where the expenses are defrayed out of the funds of the community or out of donations, the depositing owners have a chance of realising higher interest and more favorable conditions in general, than where they a must be advan- by the institution itself, great borne tage to which is secured, without les-

sening the tendency and inclination to save, by letting the interest run only from the beginning of a month or a quarter, and thus it can make a free use of the fund, deposited in the mean time. 5. It is not advisable, to limit the right of depositing to certain classes, as a has been done repeatedly, or to fix different rate of interest according to such distinctions. 6. The interest money is usually added to the capital and serves to increase it, until the owner claims the whole or a part of; still he ought to have the right of receiving the interest on demand. He ought moreover to be repaid at any time without difficulty and as soon as possible after having called in his money. 7. The safe and, at the same time advantageous investment is best secured : a, By combining the savings bank with a loan institution, standing under the same direction and management, so that both establishments should aid and assist each other. b, By purchasing the bonds of a community or the state, or by making over the funds to a public treasury; the latter measure tends very much to simplify the whole business and to secure good investment for the capitals at any time and without delay, but there are on the other hand grave disadvantages connected with it: the interest on national debts is usually lower than on other loans, and all concussions and financial embarrassments would also effect the capitals of these banks, a danger more to be dreaded in large than in small states ; one ought therefore at all events not to in

vest the entire funds of the savings banks in a national debt. c, By lending out on good mortgage, the more troublesome, but certainly the safest way. 8. Each depositor receives, after the amount of his deposit is noted in the books of the treasury and a separate book, in which the sum is put down and his interest calculated ; should it get lost, a publication to be made in the papers. 9. It is desirable, that a fund of reserve be formed in order to save eventual losses and that several persons be entrusted with the management of the funds; the treasurer has besides to give security. 10. The board of trustees must be named by those, who undertake to guarantee the deposited funds; the books, the bonds and the cash to be reviewed regularly and a yearly account of the results to be published." From the many interesting details, and statistics, contained in the notes, which accompany these I will, in consideration of the limited space of this paper, only add a few principal ones: In 1844 there were in Europe established 116!) savings banks, with a capital of about 75 millions of Spanish dollars; the oldest is one in Hamburg, founded in 1773; they have become generally known and extended in the course of the last 30 years. The savings bank, founded by parson Ducan at Ruthwell, county of Dumfries in Scotland, 1807, became the pattern of all subsequent ones; the two oldest in Germany are those of Berlin and Stuttgart, 1818. þÿ The legislature of Russia has established general rules

for all the savings banks of the whole country by (lie regulation of 12th December 1838. A British Act of Parliament ot 1833 accords to every one, who from his 20th to 30th year has deposited 5 shillings per week in a savings bank an annuity of £20 from his 60th year. St. Thomas Times, 1st May 1862. for the st. thomas times. A Bill for Compensation to the late Owners of Slaves in the Danish West India Possessions. ( Continued frir/n our last.) When we add the remittances made from St. Thomas during a series of years to those mentioned in the foregoing, it will be evident that the colonists have richly contributed to the prosperity of the Mother Country. With regard to the Island of St. Johns, we would venture to say that the state has had a sinecure; lor while the planters, until this day, have been grievously taxed with much higher imposts on their sugars and rum than the duties paid on the produce of foreign places on being introduced into St. Thomas, the expences to the state for the administration of St. Johns have been trifling. Evidence to prove that the colonists have voluntarily come forward to alleviate the sufferings of their fellow-citizens in the Parent State! Why, yes, there is the evidence of the subscriptions raised in these Islands during the last war. The amount was not very considerable, for this reason, that the colonists had likewise their losses þÿ the emancipation, drought, and convulsions in Europe. If we go back to a remoter period we will also discover that the colonists have not been backward in this respect, as port of the Bombebosse." In short it witness their contributions to the sup- " is a matter of notoriety that the inhabitants of these Islands have always readily and cheerfully contributed towards re-

lieving the distress of their fellow-men, without regard to country or nation. As it is an evil to be surrendered to the enemy, these 1 ands had their full share of affliction, 'n 1801 and 1807; trade and commerce suffered and nearly perished, while the inhabitants endured many privations. No war-tax having been imposed on us on account of the last war, we cannot certainly be reproached for not having paid any ; and how this circumstance could serve as a pretext for refusing the late slave owners compensation, we must confess we cannot perceive. Impose a war-tax on the sufferers, and exonerate those who have not suffered ! Make the slave-owner, his wife, children and creditors, the widows and orphans pay a tax of the kind, while the house-owners, capitalists, functionaries, merchants, artizans and laborers escape scot free! Why, it would be unprecedented, unjust and cruel! Another objection of Mr. David þÿ the last we shall notice here is founded on þÿ a presumption that the planters are adequately compensated by the regulations for the rural population, making it incumbent on them to enter into a contract for a specified time, fixing the hours of work, and stipulating a certain pay for their labor. This would be so, if the planters had not to pay the laborers' hire; it is, therefore, much like unlawfully dispossessing a man of his house, and giving back to him on rent. But it admitting the planters were thus compensated, would the late owners of the town slaves be thereby indemnified for

their loss? Or are their late slaves now to be brought back to a state that would be equal to bondage, as they have ever since the emancipation been as free as air? No! be generous, be just. Give back a part of the golden harvest which the Mother Country has reaped from the colonies in the days of their prosperity! Compensate the late slave-owners, and you may render both classes, planters and laborers, contented; you will thereby save the first from total ruin, and loosen the bonds which yet in some cases press

3 JT% <0 m 1 S£ heavily on the latter. You will relieve the wants and destitution of the widows and orphans ! The next member we find on the floor in opposition to the Bill is Mr. Eeiimann. For brevity sake we shall sum up the substance of the honorable gentleman's objections under the following heads: 1st. þÿ That the colonies are not so intimately connected with the Mother Country as to render the obligations existing between different parts oft he state mutual with regard to the colonies ; few of the inhabitants consider themselves as real Danish citizens; they do not dwell permanently in the colonies, where they arrive with an inconsiderable capital, for the purpose of making a fortune to return to their native countries, to which they remain attached, in language, sentiments and sympathy. 2nd. þÿ That the emancipation was not the effect of the individual act, on which the claim to indemnity is made to turn ; but it was gradually effected by the state during a long space of time, so that slavery immediately before the so-called emancipation was only a kind of domestic servitude, which possessed none of the characteristics of property. 3rd. þÿ That the question is strictly colonial, and therefore must be referred to the colonies for there to be decided, or in other words, that the colonists must bear the whole brunt of the matter. Now, with regard to the colonies not being as intimately connected with the Mother Country as all its other component parts, the fault cannot belaid at our

door, lor as the will of the Sovereign has always been law to the colonists, it entirely depended on the parent state to make the colonies an integral part of it ; and by not having done so, we have undoubtedly been the sufferers. While the Mother Country, in the days of our prosperity, has been the recipient of the surplus revenues of those Islands, we have not enjoyed the benefits of schools, colleges, hospitals, asylums for the destitute, and other benevolent and lucrative institutions, bestowed on certain parts of, and paid for by, the whole of the state. We have been treated as a tributary nation. We have been unjustly made to pay and do pay the whole of the immense expenses of the military and naval forces sent out to uphold the dignity and supremacy of the Crown, to protect the commerce and commercial fleet of the Mother Country and its inhabitaits; to pay the officers who represent the Executive power, and the functionaries who collect the customs, imposts, dues, taxes and other revenues of the state. As well may Great Britain, France, or any other power, make their subjects residing in the Empire of Hay ti, or that of China, pay for the naval forces, ambassadors, consuls and agents, sent thither to represent their respective governments, and tp protect the respective national interests. Great Britain at least does not treat her subjects in the colonies in that manner. But, says the honorable gentleman, you are not Danes. We are so by birth, by descent, by principle; not by lan-

guage þÿ some excepted ; for this simple reason, that nothing has been done by the Mother Country to encourage the study of her language, no inducements have been held out, no measures taken to disseminate her literature, to make her laws understood and generally cherished. Yet, says the honorable member, there are many strangers residing in the colo- England defrays all tlie expenses of her land and »oh forces in the colonies, besides psying the salaries namely, the Governors, Ordnance, Engineer and Commissariat Officers, l'ost-Masters, Custom-House Officers, & e þÿ En Tin

nies for the purpose only of making a fortune to return to their own native lands. Certainly, but the proportion of these foreigners in point of number to the 40,000 inhabitants of these Islands is very much like a drop of water to an ocean. Besides, the foreigners do not arrive empty handed among us, as the honorable member himself admits ; they have means to establish some business or the other ; they are compelled to become Danish burghers for the time being; they employ laborers ; they are occupy to tene- ments, for which taxes paid the state; they pay all contributions levied on their goods and other properties; they inter-marry with the natives; their children become Danes, and in their turn establish themselves in the colonies; the foreigners obey and respect the laws; they do not and cannot exclude the natives of Denmark from participating in the benefits which the commerce, trade and agriculture O of these Islands yield. > Admitting, however, all what the honorable member advances under this head with regard to the colonists be true, will the measures proposed by him tend to conciliate, to unite, to bind them to the Mother Country ? Or is there one kind of justice and equity to be meted out to our neighbours, and another kind to our kin? No! thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, is one of the Divine precepts. Thou shall deal by others as thou wishest to be dealt by, is another. ( To be continued. )

The "AVIS." Christiansted, Tuesday the 30th of March 1852. On Saturday the 27th instant, the Corner Stone of the New Church to he erected at the Moravian Establishment of Fricdensthal, near Christiansted, was laid. J lis Excellency the Governor having most graciously accepted an invitation to favor the solemnity with his presence, arrived at 12 o'clock at the dwelling house of the establishment and from thence, accompanied by a numerous ami respectable assembly ot the Authorities, Clergy and Planters of the Colony, proceeded to the site of the building, w here a dense crowd of spectators Dot ii from tow n and country was assembled. After an introductory address, the inscription to he deposited within the Corner .Stone was read and being well secured for preservation, was placed in its destined situation. The mason-work then commenced ; þÿ a trowel and some mortar being offered to His Excellency, he was graciously pleased to deliver an appropriate address, expressing in most eloquent language his benevolent wishes for the prosperity of the whole congregation attached to the Moravian mission, concluding with the usual ceremonies on such occasions. The Reverend Ki.ose, Architect ol the building, then knelt on the Cornerstone and emplored the Almighty to bestow His blessing and protection, not only on this work, but on the Island in general. The ceremony was finally concluded by singing and pronouncing the blessing.

The Norwegian Brig Antelope, of Bergen, Captain J: Svane, bound for New York with a cargo of coffee from Rio Janeiro, entered our port on the 27th instant, in distress. The Brig left Rio Janeiro on the 25th November last, and while at sea encountered a very severe gale, which caused considerable damage to her masts, sails and rigging. One of the crew was unfortunately lost, and the Captain was compelled to throw overboard 455 bags of coffee, to lighten his vessel. We understand she will lie refitted here and proceed on her voyage.

A portion of the property belonging to the heirs of the late king Louis Philippe, was put up to sale on the 14th ult., in the civil tribunal of first instance of the department of the Seine, with all the formalities required by the law. The property was composed of three lots, and was sold for 1 1 1,100 francs. The sale attracted a considerable number of persons, no doubt in consequence of the decree of confiscation of the 23rd of January. It may he right, however, to observe, that the sale of yesterday was without reference, and it may be said, notwithstanding that decree; and the fact of its not having been arrested by the law officers of the government in consequence of that decree has appeared strange, and, in fact, inexplicable to the friends of the princes of the Orleans family. The sale was decided on before the decree in question. The Independanee of Brussels publishes a model petition, which the supporters of Louis Napoleon are circulating for signature, in order to its presentation to the senate upon its meeting. The prayer of the petition is, that Louis Napoleon may graciously assume the empire, and constitute it hereditary, in order to assure France against evils which she is now dreading. The first petition emanates from the town of Chatillon-sur- Loire. The Monifcur, of the 18th ult.. publishes the law on the press. No paper is to be created without Government authority. Political newspapers published in foreign countries are not to he

allowed to circulate in France without Government authority. The cautionmoney of a paper appearing more than thrice a-week to be 50,000 francs. All publication of a paper without authority, or without lodging the caution-moncy, is to he punished with a fine of from 100 to 2,000 francs for each number, and imprisonment of from one month to two years. The stamp duties imposed on newspapers are also applicable to foreign newspapers, unless they are exempted under a diplomatic convention. Correctional jurisdiction is substituted for jury. One condemnation for crime, or two condemnations for a contravention, cause suspension. Articles arc not required to be signed. The centime stamp on the Roman feuilleton is retained. Booksellers are obliged to obtain a license." Lord Cowley, the new British Ambas sador to the French Republic, arrived in Paris on the 17th. He alighted at the Hotel Bristol, Place Vendome. To Mr. " Philo-Rigby f Sir, þÿ Although your fair production clearly bears the marks ot Caliban, yet as even he was not insensible, I will in charity presume, that a few serious words addressed to you will not be without effect. Your indirect defence of "the awkward integrity" of your friend " Rigby," however it may speak in favor of your heart, does little credit to your head. Neither your Billingsgate eloquence, surpassing in foulness that of Thersites and Timon, nor your low cunning in avoiding to come to the point, has failed in bringing down upon you the censure of every lover of truth, decency, and morality. " Philo-Rigby," Your assumption of the name of is not happier than your styling your friend Jean qui rit. Had you been aware of the qualities, which Junius gives Rigby, I am certain you would not as you style our " Rigby ;" Jean qui rit, have called yourself a lover of " Rigby," you, who ly are " Jean qui plevre." Now we are are "Philo-Rigby" consequenttold in Scott's historical novel of Quentin Durward, that the assistants of the notorious finisher of the law, Tristan 1' Ilermite, were thus called. How far both of you are deserving of bearing the names of these worthies, I leave it to your sober judgment to reconsider. Our " Rara A vis's" being verdantly green amuses you highly ; is it on account of your friend being cured t If you be not green, it must be confessed, that your talents are such as any one, who has stolen the property of another, may safely hire to defend his cause, þÿ provi-

ded that the case is to be tried in Bedlam, to the region of which your burning eloquence seems to be peculiarly adopted ; although you may be more knave than fool. Now Sir, should these few serious observations have the effect of reforming you and your Prototype, I shall deem myself peculiarly happy in having effected a miracle ; for 1 believe that not even "contempt" will pierce your hearts. For the St. Croix Avis. That artful wag, "Philo-Rigby", whoever he may be, must be vastly delighted with the success of his hoax. The trap was well set, and, as he anticipated, the credulous Editor of the "St. Thomae Tidende" has fallen in the snare. Labouring " Philo-Rigby's", rather under the impression, that obscene, we must confess, but apt epithets were bestowed on us, and that the public approved thereof, the unsuspecting Editor lias been induced to attempt brazing over his clever feat. In his invaluable paper of the 24th inst. he has responded exactly in the manner, that the ingenious contriver of the snare expected. The immaculate Editor, suffering under the poisonous effects of the bait which he had swallowed, has imputed our motive to malice, for branding his keen trick with its merited stigma. Now, admitting even that we were actuated by malice, would that justify him for reprinting another's work without his consent, and then vain-gloriously boasting of it ? But as we possess too high a degree of contempt for him, we are incapable of bearing malice against him. happy as to find many, among others The dupe pretends to have been so " some very respectable men," (" Philo-Rigbys,") who are of his opinion. Were this true, it would not be surprising to us ; Diogenes at mid-day, with a taper, could not find an honest man ! It is not uncommon for a man to do so often thaKt which is wrong, till at last

he fancies it to he right. His ideas of mine and thine become so perverted, that it requires severe measures to convince him of his evil doings. Such appears to be the state of the Editor ; the declares, that he is as innocent as he babe unborn! If this assertion impugn his veracity þÿ what shall we say of his understanding? How can we believe, that he holds himself guiltless, when in reprinting the translation, he branded the deed as not honest, in his paper, " unfair?" " Pah ! the offence is rank ; it smells to heaven !" The Editor taking, howduped by the ever, for granted, that the " public will be hoax of Philo-Rigby," and by his own verbiage, indulges himself in a flight to the upper regions. And if a metaphysical jargon be a proof of inspiration, it would seem, that he has been inspired with a vengeance. Like the oracles of ancient Greece he pours forth his inspirations in the following perspicuous strain : " That newspapers, therefore, or those who conduct them, should occasionally incur unmerited hatred for treating of things, the mere mention of which damages the easily-earned position of those who would continue in its enjoyment, could the newspaper but remain the waste sheet it used to be, and dumb and blind to every passing circumstance, is a very natural consequence; but having taken upon itself to say a few words, enemies assail it, and are ready to strike it low." Match me ye climes ! Where shall we lind a piece of eloquence to equal this rare specimen of the Editor's talents ?

The value of which is enhanced a hundred fold ; as " the torrid zone (in the language of Mrs. Malaprop) is not prolific hi books, nor cerebral activity." He it as it may, the Editor's outpourings may pass as a poetical fiction; he himself does not believe, that he is a martyr in the cause of" Truth and Justice." We at least will not believe it, unless he proves what reforms he has attempted, and what persecutions he has suffered. When the Editor adds: "We are, nevertheless, at our post, and intend continuing to review men and things, with truth and justice," we must consider it as another of his fictions. It our Editor " really men and things," why state, he will do intend, in future, to dzidfuirly with so without " fear of retaliation ?" This appears to be a mental reservation. We hope, however, that our suspicion is illgrounded ; for who according to the old adage will be better able to catch trespassers on the manor of literature, than he V As we do not, however, intend for the present to take this opportunity of going further into the details connected with the several protestations of the Editor's sham innocence with regard to malice 011 his said just enough part, we rest to satisfied show " what with having appears yet to be his notions of Truth and Justice." 27th March 1852. Mr. Editor, As an inhabitant of Santa Cruz and therefore one deeply concerned in its prosperity; as a Christian and therefore bound to raise my voice when the honor and glory of God is in question, I am constrained to add a little to my communication of last week, which you were kind enough to give a place in your paper. I am well aware of the custom that has alas ! too long prevailed in these Islands with those transferred from their distant homes, to forget early impressions ; what an anxious father counsel-

<0 1ft <© 1 S£ AT IS. led ; what a loving mother taught, and with minds wholly set upon ungodly gain to think little of the pernicious effect of their example upon others, whose means of instruction has been more limited. From whence has arisen (what every one who believes in God or an hereafter must deplore) forgetfulness ot the great Jehovah, carelessness about religion and profanation of the Holy day of rest. If there is one place more than another where the voice of God should be heard in His works, it is here ; for what is the most careful management; what the most improved agriculture ; what the best machinery which the inventive genius of man ever contrived, without the early and the latter rain. Can the Sabbath breaker expect a blessing from God upon hisendeavors? I think not. The observance of the Sabbath is the mark of a Christian people; it was early instituted ; it was stringently commanded ; the breach of it severely punished. On the Sabbath we celebrate the great deliverance ot man from a bondage worse than that of Egypt ; the abuse of the Sabbath ; the finding our own pleasure ; the doing our own ways 011 the day of rest which God claims for Himself, is open and avowed infidelity ; is a denial of the faith which has elevated nations in the social scale. What is the foundation of the strength and wealth ot mighty England? What is the secret of the -rapid progress of England's sons in the new world ? Christianity. For where the one would exercise her power, she plants the holy banner. Where

the others would subdue the giant oaks of the forest to the hand of þÿman they build a church. Look at France, the infidel worshippers of the Goddess of reason, what are they, with their boasted liberty and equality ? Every thing that is dear to them depends for safety upon the imperial nod of a tyrant. We have many in God's house 011 his day 1 would þÿ raise the indignation of such against the insult their Christianity receives from those who do the evil þÿthing Sunday store whose owner abjures buying and Sunday selling. his Taboo Christian the name for stivers. Eat not Sunday bread, lest it should be like the Sunday manna of wilderness þÿ full of worms. Join me ye that value your Christian caste; that Sabbath profanation may be put down, then may we hope that the fruitful land which has become barren, may again teem with that plenty which Santa Cruz in more favored days has known. 1 am, Mr. Editor, Yours &c. A West-Ender. March 31st, 1852. « Wilmer and Smith's European 'Times, March 1, 1852. SPAIN. Our accounts from Madrid are of the lltli ultimo. The last bulletin of the Queen's health states that Her Majesty's position continued most satisfactory. The Queen still manifested the desire of repairing to the Church of Atocha on the 15th. The weather was inclement, and the physicians considered her Majesty too feeble to undertake that pilgrimage. They, the the emotion which moreover, dreaded enthusiastic reception she would experience on that day might produce. Nevertheless the

preparations were making as if the ceremony was to take place. Accounts from Madrid, of the 18th, describe the pilgrimage of the Queen to the church of Atocha. At half-past two o'clock a salute of artillery announced the departure of the Queen from the palace. Twenty young girls, dressed in white, carrying garlands of flowers, and preceded by a band of music, opened the march, and were followed by

the rich equipages of the Spanish grandees. Nextcame twelve court carriages, drawn each by four horses, and in which were seated the officers of the Queen's household, and the carriages of the Infanta Don Francisco de Paula, father of the King, escorted by a detachment of cavalry. The Duke and Duchess of Montpensier, who followed, rode in a landau, the taste and richness of which were only exceeded by the carriage of the Queen. Her Majesty held in her arms the Princess Royal, and was accompanied by the King and the nurse of the infant Princess. As the royal equipage advanced, flowers and devices were thrown down from the windows, doves were let fly, and the cries of " Viva la Reina!" mingled with the roaring of the artillery. The Queen looked well, and appeared delighted with her enthusiastic reception. The procession was closed by the authorities of Madrid and a squadron of cavalry. At the church of Atocha her Majesty was received by deputations of the Grandees, of the Senate and Chamber of Deputies, and the municipal corporations. The most perfect order prevailed. The Queen was present at night at a representation in the Theatre del Principe, which was extremely brilliant. The enthusiasm of the auditory was not less than that manifested by the population in the streets. The city was splendidly illuminated. The Square del Oriente, lighted up with upwards of (30,000 tapers, presented a most magic aspect. The people continued to crowd the streets during the whole night, and

order was not for an instant disturbed. The Queen held a grand levee in the Hall of the Ambassadors. Her Majesty wore a rich diadem, and received everybody with her usual grace. The Queen was to give a grand ball on the night of the 10th.

Accounts from Berlin, dated the 21st ultimo, state that a political trial, to which the high position and abilities of the accused have lent much interest, had taken place that day in that city. Count Henry Arnim, a member of the First Prussian Chamber : a titular Minister of State, formerly Minister of Foreign Affairs, and who had also represented his King at the court of Versailles and in Belgium, was placed at the criminal bar, and accused of calumniating the government by his writings. Count Henry Arnim is a leader of the liberal party. When M. Manteuflel went to Olmutz, in 1850, and there surrendered to Prince Schwarzenberg every principle of policy which favourably distinguished Prussia from her despotic rival ; when he gave up the Union, and accepted the detested Diet ; when he abandoned llesse-Cassel, and permitted Austrians to march to Hamburg, Henry Arnim published a pamphlet, called "The Policy of the Counter-Ilevolutions; two speeches, spoken and unspoken." From this pamphlet were derived certain passages upon which were based the charge of exciting to hatred and contempt of the Ministry. With Count Arnim was arraigned M. Bardesleben, formerly editor of the Constitutionelle, who had reprinted in his journal a portion of the incriminated discourse. The court condemned the Count to pay a fine of 200 thalers, or be imprisoned four months, and M. Bardesleben to pay 100 thalers, or suffer two months' imprisonment. The substitution of a fine,

for the absolute imprisonment required by the prosecution turns upon the fact that the Count was found guilty, not of the calumny imputed, but merely of offensive reference to the Minister. This is the first time a Minister of State has ever hcen arraigned in Prussia. An appeal is spoken of. þÿ Ibid.

We are sensible lliat our readers will feel some interest in the perusal of the following letters from Colonel IIaasum, Governor of St. Bartholomew, to Mr. I)e Gout, acknowledging the receipt of his letter conveying advices of the sum collected in this Island lor the relief of the sufferers. And we have some satisfaction in stating that the amount has since been considerably augmented in this Island, þÿ without including a sum of about 8800, collected by the same gentleman in the Sister-Island of St. Croix. Also will he found published below a letter to the Secretary of State at Stockholm, acquainting I lis Excellency ot the unfortunate calamity which had befallen one of the Swedish Possessions: Government-! louse, St. Bartholomews, ) .March 18th, 185:1. \ To Joseph De Gout, Esq., St. Thomas. Sir! I will not delay a moment to acknowledge the receipt, late last evening, of your highly esteemed letter of the 1.1th instant, communicating the gratifying intelligence ot the sympathy manifested in your Island for the sufferers by the calamitous Eire of the '2nd instant, and which resulted in the very munificent collection of One thousand six hundred Dollars you announce. For your praise-worthy, zealous, and indefatigable exertions in behalf ol'your former fellow-citizens, and which have been crowned with such signal success, accept my warmest thanks, as well as those of this community, and convey the same to your worthy Governor, and the irenerons Inhabitants of St. Thomas, who

so readily and liberally responded to your Appeal. May the consciousness of your good deed lie your reward, for we can only appreciate it, and may Heaven shield you and the benevolent Subscribers from similar misfortunes. \\ e are slowly recovering from the tirst shock of this most calamitous event þÿ and we have had the consolation to receive evidences of the warm sympathy s of the benevolent communities around us, particularly Guadeloupe, whose Inhabitants have promptly come to our reli< f w ith large supplies of money and clothing. In conformity with your request, I have litis day drawn on you a Bill at sight to the order of Kirhard Dirizey, Esq., for the above $ I and tit the suggestion of that gentleman, I have, in the letter of advice accompanying the Draft, requested you to pay any further amount that may subsequently have been collected by you to Mr. M. Eevcrork, w hose receipt w ill be valid as a remittance. My manifold occupation at this moment will, I trust, serve as an apology for these hurried lines. ! remain, with great respect, Sir, Your most obedient servant, JAMES II. IIAASUM.

Sir ! The distressing character of the present communication I hope will, in some measure excuse the step I take in placing a statement connected therewith before Your Excellency. Whilst the conviction of the extent of sympathy and commisseration with which I anticipate it will be received offers to me the assurance that Your Excellency will pardon my individual anxiety in behalf of the Inhabitants of St. Bartholomew, whose afflictions and present condition have aroused the sympathy of the people here, and that of the neighbouring Islands. On the 2nd instant, the principal portion ot' the 3rd section of the Town of' Gustavia was destroyed by a conflagration, which baffled in the outset all attempts made to subdue or arrest its progress. The Fire was discovered at 2 o'clock in the morning, the flames spread w ith fearful rapidity and destructive effect, and the Morning Sun rose over the smoking ruins of Two Hundred Buildings, and A BEGGARED I' EOF EE ! ! ! The hapless inmates, driven by the fire, fled from house to house, thence to the beach and as many as the vessels could give shelter to were hurried on board. In their flight, the fugitives abandoned all they possessed; the sentiments of self-preservation, the love of life, the ties of kindred, proved superior to all consideration of property or interest ; therefore the scene of misery and desolation is complete. Immediately on the receipt of the disastrous intelligence, notwithstanding the absence of the details, I addressed an

Appeal to the Inhabitants of St. Thomas; the Community have noblv responded to that Appeal. I hold to-day the sum of One Thousand Eight Hundred Spanish Dollars, for the sufferers, as will appear from the accompanying number of the St. Thomas Tidende, 17th March 1852. From the benevolent exertions ofColonel II. VV. Precht, K. D., and some of the ladies, members of the Benevolent Association of St. Thomas, some further supplies have been collected for the sufferers. Additional efforts will be made in the neighbouring Islands to obtain if possible some temporary relief, and my strenuous exertions will be devoted to that object. The high and distinguished character of the present Administration, of which Colonel J. II. llaasum is the Chief; the honorable standing of the community of the Town of Gustavia, either in a moral point of view, or in their commercial intercourse abroad could not fail to establish a favorable impression among their neighbours þÿ a circumstance worthy of the attention of HIS MAJESTY'S GOVERNMENT, and the ESTEEM OF THE SWEDISH NATION þÿ! hence the respectful sympathy and sorrow with which the sad announcement of the calamity has been received in the For-
eign Islands. With sentiments of deep respect, I have the honor to be, Your Excellency's most obdt. sevt. JOS. DkGOUT

Infanticide We are much grieved, but nevertheless feel it our duty, to report a circumstance of the most inhuman and cold-blooded nature that has disgraced society within the last eight days þÿ which we omitted to notice on Wednesday þÿ and it is no less than the heinous crime of Infanticide. On Sunday morning last the body of a female infant, supposed, from its fresh appearance, not to have been many hours old, was observed floating about the wharf of Messrs. Osorio, Wright, &. Casseres. The lifeless remains of the poor innocent were taken up, and removed to the Island Hospital, where an Inquisition was held over the same by Doctors Pedersen (King's Physician), and Magens, who, we are informed, were of opinion that the child had been born alive the night before, or that very morning, and that it was drowned, as no marks of violence were perceptible by which strangulation could have been effected. The cruel creature þÿ nay, monster! þÿ who could have been accomplice to this sinful act must feel deeply the anguish of a guilty conscience, for the blood of the innocent cries aloud for vengeance! "Is there a crime heneath the roof ot Heaven, that stains the soul of woman, with more infernal hue, than damn'd Infanticide?" Or "who would rend the screaming infant from the breast to plunge it in the sea?" "Heaven and Earth doth cry impossible, but Hell doth know it true." We beg leave to call the attention of our readers to the appeal of the Spanish Consul at St. Thomas, to the inhabitants of the Danish Antilles, for their pecuni arv aid to lonnd charitable institutions, tor the poor and destitute in the Spanish Capital þÿ a plan suggested by lier Ma jesty Queen ISABELLA, in commemoration of that event, which litis given Spain a Princess and a future Sovereign. W e are well aware of the straitened circumstances of our planters anil tin community in general ; but as a gift must be judged of by the motive which acta ates the giver and not by the magnitude of the gift, we trust that no one, on the plea of not being able to give much, will refuse his mite, to enable the Spanish Government to carry out this benevolent suggestion. We, as all must confess, owe much n the Spanish Government, for their as sistancc in 1848, when our lives and pro perties were in imminent danger. But for 1 his assistance, so promptly rendered, the properties of all might have been ruined and their owners beggared. This debt of gratitude, w hich we owe, may now, at least in part, he repaid, and we hope, therefore, that this appeal will not be in vain. Mr. Editor þÿ although very few books make their appearance before the public without a prelace, jet I believe but very few persons read it. Now, in this respect I beg leave to differ from the practise of the majority. 1 almost invariably read first what first presents itself to the reading faculties. 1 have done so with the "Historical Account" of three of the Danish West India Islands. I need not say to you that the perusal has afforded me a large amount of the most exquisite pleasure: and 1 suppose I ought to regret that, as yet, the preface is the only portion of the work that I have been able to go right through with. Unlike most historic writers þÿ the author of the " Account" not only narrates, but also amuses. He keeps the mind perpetually on the watch. lie does not commence an idea, and then hold it with the tenacious determination never to let it go. He does not spin it out þÿ turn it and twist it, and elongate it þÿ as if the metamorphosing of one idea would atone lor the introduction of no other. In this our author is independent and original. He forsakes the hard beaten pathway of the multitude, goes forth info a region unexplored, carrying with him his most willing reader, enraptured with delight. The two opening sentences are full of the striking and amusing. The author cannot admit the idea that " if a work be good it needs no apology ; if bad it deserves none." Now this bespeaks the

lofty independence of the author, lie disdains what other men admire; and hence he discards this puerile "idea," which has become axiomatic with a eertaiu e/ass ot authors. A "good work" does need an þÿapology notwithstanding some dupes think it does not ; and v. v. a bad work does deserve an apology. We like this opposition of different ideas: like that of flint and steel, it often is valuable for the production of latent light. Another prominent peculiarity in this sentence deserves our notice. It is the rather unusual employment of the capital A. Of all things most despicable is prudery, or assumed modesty. So we think ; and were much gratified indeed to find that our view is undesignedly adopted by the Author , before us. Many prudish men would have affected the modesty ot using the minor a. Most authors deem theirs to be but common appellations. This one author (Author) is very proper in not following the deceptions of the fraternity. But we must proceed to sentence the second. Yielding to a sillv habit we once acquired by reading Euclid and þÿUegendre we supposed this next sen-

Z U\ <0 Ui >0 I a ATI a» tence would have contained, or commenced, a defence of the beligerent position which our author had assumed in the first. Our simplicity was in supposing this the proper and logical order of the discourse. Hence upon a first reading we were a little puzzled to find or follow the connection. Now it would have been natural for most writers to cling to the first, leading, opposing idea, and to have secured it, or attempted to secure it, by some clinchers immediately " succeeding. rises superior" to such a vulgar proce- Our Author, however, dure. Why should he not rather with his own peculiar originality, just simply ask þÿ : "May there not be an intermediate state between good and bad to which circumstances doom the writings of many and to which they would gladly have risen superior had it been in their power." Now suppose Wu.vTEi.EY, or Watts, or Parker, or Aristotle þÿ should pronounee this illogical : what have they to do with the work of an original thinker, it he differ from them without deigning " to render a reason ?" Interrogation is often much better than argument ; because, you can easily ask questions that yourself or no other one can answer. However, we do not say it is thus here. Coleridge avers that poetry has a "logic ot' its own." Now ii" parson k's prose possess the same priviliged quality þÿ whose business is it? For ourselves, we like it. II en and Women. A woman is naturally gratified when a man singles her out, and addresses his conversation to her. She takes pains to appear to the best advantage, but without any thought of willfully misleading. How different is it with men ! At least it is thus that women in general think of men. The mask with them is deliberately put on and worn as a mask, and wo betide the silly girl who is too weak or too unsuspicious, not to appear displeased with the well-turned compliments and flatteringattentions so lavishly bestowed upon her by her partner .at the ball. If a girl has brothers she sees a little behind the scenes, and is saved much mortification and disappointment. She discovers how little men mean byattentions they so freely bestow upon the last new face which takes their fancy. Men are singularly wanting in good feeling upon this subject; they pay a girl marked attention, flatter her in every way, and then, perhaps, when warned by some judicious friend that they arc going too far, "can hardly believe the girl could be so foolish as to fancy that any thing was meant."

So long as the discovery of gold in Austra iia evinced merely the same features as those I with which the public had already become familiar in California we fell li tie reason for serious alarm, and regarded the distress and ptessuie to which existing inleiests in the colony were subjected as the necessary ordeal through which they were destined to puss before they could arrive it a permanent state of higher prosperity. Looking with some dislavour upon the exclusive employment of the resources of the c entry m the production of wool to the neglect of all other means of developing its riches, and regarding with disapprobation the manner in which the Colonial-office had handed over so many millions of acres to the proprietors of flocks and herds under the eX| r< ss condition that the land should not he cultivated, we were not sorry to see a new . o. a lion arise which might in some degree > 'e the excessive power of the dominant pas'oral interest. That a few men capable enduring hardship of

and great personal fatigue should be enabled to procure for their labour a considerably higher remuneration than they could obtain in private employment appeared by no means j a subject of þÿ- get, more especially when it was remembeied that the discovery of Australian gold-fielda would arrest the emigration from there to California, would provide the colony with a fresh commodity of þÿexport and probably attract towards it a considerable number of enterprising and hardy adventurers, well fined either in the mine or forest to act as the pioneers of civilization and the explorers of wealth. This view of the subject seems, however, to be completely altered by the latest accounts from the gold mines of Victoria. It is gravely stated that the average earnings of a miner in this favoured locality are not less than twelve hundred a year, and that there appears to be an almost boundless quantity of the precious metal to be had tor the taking. Making any reasonable deduction for the possible exaggeration of these accounts, the tesult is still sufficiently formidable. The property which must be sacrificed in the shape of flocks and herds alone is enormous Sheep and cattle require daily labour to preserve them in a country where fences are unknown and personal superintendence alone relied upon. Even to melt them into tallow requires an amount of manual labour which under existing circumstances cannot be commanded. The fleece oi lust October was shorn, for that was before the discovery or

general knowledge of the extraordinary riches of Bort Philip ; but to what labour ate we to look to obtain for the colonists the fleece which in five months will be ready for the shearer ? It is not merely the amount of the capital to be destroyed that we have to consider ; we must also remember the time which will be required to replace it To produce the enormous ft >cks and herds which now roam over 'be plains of Australia has required the energy "id intelligence of nearly half the century btch has elapsed since the .Merino sheep »a» first introduced into that congenial cltoate. If this stock be allowed to perish, it will require many years to renew, even allowing for a rate of increase stimulated by the most favourable circumstances. Thecultivation of the vine is making the most rapid nod encouraging progress ; all the finest kinds are already domesticated, and year by year the vintage evinces a steady improvement- The vineyards must, we apprehend, neces sarilv be allowed to run wild, and a single þÿyear neglect s will destroy the germ of a product wtiich was fust advancing to excellence. The gardens, the peculiar pride of the colonists, where the products of the temperate and torrid zone flourish side by side, must be surrendered to devastation, and premature decay will rapidly replace precocious deveiopement. þÿGoldsmith s Deserted þÿVillage to was a melancholy but imaginary picture; how much sadder to see the early promise of civilization blighted in the bud than to dwell

on its possible extinction after it shall have attained its full proportions ! If we turn from the material to the moral and intellectual effects of the change, the prospect is equally repulsive and disheartening. Intellectual labour is seldom highly rewarded or justly estimated in new countries, but in the state of things about to commence in Australia it will be absolutely at a discount.

A T 'i 8. The successful barrister or physician can j hardly hope to obtain an income equal to that which may be secured by a person merely endowed with the attribute of animal strength. The clergyman must content himself with a small fraction of the income of the day labourer, the skilled mechanic will receive a far lower remuneration for the exercise of his trade than the convict who has learnt dexterity in the use of the pickaxe j from labouring on the roads or other public works The estimate of the dignity of an occupation will follow in a great degree the amount of its reward. If brute strength be found more lucrative than trained skill or practised intellect, it is in a fair way to be more highly regarded. Such a state of things recalls the ru le beginnings of society j and tends to undo all that civilization may previously have effected. The poor will become rich, and the rich poor, and a total inversion of opinions is but too likely to follow the change itt the relative estimation of classes. We cannot wholly remedy this slate of things. We can as little prevent greedy hands from being stretched out to reap the golden harvest as we can compel the teeming earth to withhold her treasures. But what can be done in the wav of palliation ought to be attempted without loss of time. We pride ourselves on a reduction of the number of ablebodied paupers now piningin compulsory idleness throughout the country ; but is it to i be tolerated that our finest possessions should thus be destroyed before our eyes entirely

for want of labout when in England alone 137.000 adult persons are still in receipt of patish relief? To allow such a stale of things to continue would be an indelible disgrace to our national character, and a practical denial of the Existence of statesman- , ship even of the huinbliest order among us. Is it so utterly beyond the powers of the human mind to devise the means of remedying this inequality and of feeding t he scarcity of one part of the empire with t he redundancy ol another ? Is it only for the purposes of war and destruction that Governments can transfer large masses of the human race from the shores of one continent to the shores of another ? Is there enterprise enough in tins count i v to send forth missionaries to starve on the storm-beaten rocks of Cape Horn, but not enough to convey paupers to become rich on the golden plains of Australia ? If we could spend five millions in 1851 to perpetuate poverty and misery in this land, might we not spare one million in 1852 to remove that poverty and misery for ever, even though the process should be attended with the result of saving the Australian colonics from destruction? We have the land revenues of Australia and the Boor Kates of England, an ample fund on which to secure the interest of any loan required for the purpose, and it would not be difficult, considering the unexampled facility of earning money in Australia, obtain from the emigrant the repayment of the greatest portion of his passage-money. This latter object would be especially facilita-

ted by an alteration in the law which should render unnecessary the heavy notarial charges and the stamp payable on such an agreement þÿ an alteration by which two pounds could be saved in the case of every emigrant binding himself to any terms to be performed in the colonics. Without the loss of a single shilling to the public the large capital in Austialia now threatened with destruction might be preserved, the pressure of the Boor

Katesat home permanently alleviated, ai d the production of wealth enormously increased. A little while and the opportunity will be past, and the task of settling our þÿAus raliat, colonies must be almost commenced a new-

þÿi ORT OF SPAIN : FRIDAY, MAY 7, 1852. It is with sincere and poignant regret we announce the death of His Grace, Archbishop Smith. His Grace's usually excellent health had been known to have been impaired for some months past ; but it was only a fortnight ago that the symptoms that have terminated so fatally, first manifested themselves; since then, Doctors Court and Satuunin have been in constant attendance at the Archepiscopal residence, and nothingihai medical skill could effect was neglected to avert the impending danger, and prolong a life so invaluable to the very large portion of this community over whom His Grace's pastoral charge extended. Brayers for his recovery were also offered up in the Roman Catholic Cathedral of this Town, and several of the rural Parishes ; bui medical skill and the supplications to the Throne of Grace of his very large congregation were alike unavailing; and at 3 p. m., yesterday afternoon, the lolling of the Cathedral bells announced to the inhabitants of Bort of Spain that the soul of the worthy Brelate had left its frail tenement of clay and was winging its way, let us hope, to that other and better world, þÿ where the wicked þÿ cease from troubling, and where the weary þÿ are at þÿrest. Preparations, we understand, are being made for the preservation of the corpse, until the arrival of the Right Reverend Dr. Monaghan, R 0. Bishop of Roseau, who is expected here in the next Steamer, (on a visit to the Archbishop) and on whom will devolve the painful task of celebrating the funeral

obsequies of his lamented friend and ecclesiastical superior. The funeral, we understand, will take place, (D. V.), on Wednesday morning next, at 8 þÿo clock and, (independent of the numbers whom curiosity will undoubtedly draw together on such an occasion) the þÿArchbishop r s emains will, we doubt þÿnot be followed to their last resting place, not only by the sorrowing members of his own Church, but by the very many of on Brotestant inhabitants, to whom Dr Smith d endeared to himself, by his extreme an of manners, and truly liberal sentiment As an opportunity will be afforded us, in recording the departed þÿBrelate s funeral obsequies, of returning to the subject, we prefer, (especially in the crowded state of our columns), deferring to that opportunity the tribute we think due from us as a conductor of the public press to the character of a man who has so long occupied a more important pluce in the public estimation of this Colony. Valentin Canedo, nominated, by Her Majesty the Queen, Civil Supeiior and Captain-General of the Island, took possession, on the 1 6th iust., of his high office. The honorable antecedents of the public life of His Excellency, give us the greatest hope that he will know how to worthily answer the favor of our august sovereign, in being for Cuba an authority as intelligent and active as right. Wishing not to stain our lips with vulgar adulations, we should not express such sentiments if we were not firmly convinced of their truth. THE DEPARTURE OF GEN. CONCHA. His Excellency, senior Lieutenaut-General 1). Jose de la Concha, departed on the 16th inst , from the port of Havana, in the steamer Isabel la Catolica, for the Peninsula. The remembrance ol his administration that General Concha has engraved in the memory of Cuba, is able to satisfy tfie highest aspirations of a just pride. As a good and loyal Spaniard, as a gentleman and as the first authority. His Excellency merited and obtained the unanimous appreciation of al' the inhabitants of our island. Feeble but faithful echos of the opinion, with which our daily business put us always in communication, we can affirm that the profoundest sympathy and the warmest desire for his future happiness, will accompany General Concha on his return from Cuba to the mother coun-
try.

Marriage of Jenny Lind. The following extract from a letter lias recently appeared in print, giving some of the particulars of Jenny Lind's marriage to Otto Goldschmidt, a young German artist, to whom she was tenderly attached. The writer says: þÿ "She asked me to draw up her marriage contract, gave me the particulars how she wished her property to be settled, &,c., which was done in due form ; and in connexion herewith, I will mention, that, with that high spirit of generosity that has always marked to her cha- a racter, she set apart þÿ. ¬20,00(1 found Charity School in Sweden. Last Wednesday 1 went to Boston, and she approved of the marriage contract; and the next day, the 5th inst., she was married to Mr. Goldschmidt, at the house of Mr. Ward, a friend of hers and Goldschmidt's. The morning was bright and cloudless, and prognosticated well for her marriage state. She was dressed in white silk, with a veil, and orange flower wreath, intermingled with myrtle a la Suedoise, with a bouquet or corsage of the same, and looked very charming. The queries were pronounced by the Itev. Dr. Wainwright, a clergyman from New York, whom she had invited for the purpose. Only half a dozen friends were present ; among them Mr. Everitt, who was Minister to London a few years ago. Then came the kissing of the bride, performed by the staid guests by imprinting a beneficial kiss on the forehead, except by one whom Jenny embraced, and gave an old-fashioned Swedish kiss. She seemed a very Amina,

so joyous, so happy, stepping on air as it were. Alter a while she sat down to the piano, and sang 'Ah non giunge,' wit ha heartiness that would have brought the whole Opera House at her feet. In the afternoon they went off to a country seat at Northampton, about 100 miles from Boston, which they hired for a few months. In the summer they return to Europe. Mr. Goldschmidt isseven years younger than herself þÿ about 24 years old, a small, very good-looking man, of a high-toned character, well-educated, and devoted to her. lie is from Hamburg, where his father is a respected merchant." þÿ Observer.

Economy in Dental Operations. þÿ A farmer of the neighbourhood of Boulogne, in France, applied the other day to a dentist of that city, and complained of severe pain in a decayed tooth. The dentist told him that the tooth would bear stopping with lead, and asked him to return in a few days. When the farmer had returned home, he thought that he might save the dentist's fee, and asked the blacksmith of the village to pour some melted lead into the tooth. The worthy knight of the anvil did as he was bid, and the poor farmer saved bis money, but had almost the whole ot one side of his jaw burnt away.
