The "AVIS." Christiansted, Tuesday the 1st of June 1852. The St. Croix Savings Bank was opened on Saturday last at 1 o'clock p. in., to receive deposits, as previously announced in our papers. The Receivers were : II. L. Arnesen Esq., , Trustee; Joseph Abbott , and J. If. Burt , Esquires, Members. A number ot depositors presented themselves, and it is pleasing to us to state that the deposits amounted to $ 190. The hours ol business are from 1 to 3 p. m., which we consider a very inconvenient time for mechanics, servants, and the country people. Mechanics do not leave their work before 1 o'clock in the afternoon, and consequently can not come sooner to make their deposits; servants are also prevented from being present in the afternoon these people are, therefore, obliged þÿ to avail themselves of the advantages of the Institution þÿ to , entrust their savings D to others to deposit tor them, which can not be as gratifying to them, as if they deposited their money themselves. We would therefore suggest that the hours ot business he altered, hi order to enable the working classes to come personally and make their own deposits. If this were done, we are of opinion, a great many more persons would he induced to become depositors.

The Observer, April 18, 1852. Mir J. Franklin's Expedition. The statement that has been running the round of the journals, and which will be found in another part of The Observer þÿ the discovery of two namely, ships on an iceberg in the Atlantic last spring (1851) þÿ would seem to set at rest the fate of Sir J. Franklin and his followers. This statement, so far as it goes, hears about it all the characteristics of truth ; for it is not only substantially indentical, when stated by different witnesses, but there is a printed record of the fact in a respectable local newspaper þÿ the Limerick Chrovicle þÿ published almost immedi-

ately after the singular spectacle presented by the floating grave had been witnessed The concurrent testimony of several persons fixes the date of this event as on the 20th April, 1851, and on the 28th May following the Limerick Chronicle contained the record in question, which was couched in the form of a letter from a passenger, dated Quebec, on the 8th of the same month. Doubts have been cast on the statement of the principal witness, Mr. Simpson, then chief mate of the Renovation, merchantman, now master of the British Queen, bark, engaged in the Canada to impute to him the faculty called " see- trade ; and it has been sought indirectly ing double" þÿ a faculty certainly not uncommon with shippers of all kinds navigating high latitudes. But, independent of the fact that no imputation of insobriety rests upon the character of this gentleman, the theory of double reflection advanc ed to account for the appearance of these two ships on the ice is completely nullified by the doctrine of polarisation as regards light; while the independent statement of the passenger just alluded to sets at rest all cavil on score of certainty. It is true that Franklin's fate occupied to a considerable extent the public mind at the period refer red to ; it is also true that the supposed catastrophe of the expedition was the subject of general conversation both in America and England; and therefore it is not unreasonable to assume that the lapse of time since the ships in question

were seen on the iceberg without any mention of the matter is a strong argument against the probability of the story. But, on the other hand, it must be borne in mind that seafaring men live almos' entirely within their own narrow circle þÿ that for the irreater part they are ignorant of what is passing in the world þÿ that they are almost constantly at sea, cut off from all communication with their kind, or if ashore that they are most frequently what þÿ strong drink is termed "muddled" with and that, generally speaking, they are the least observant, most incurious, and, on the whole, most unintelligent portion of mankind. The majority of them are taken from "before the mast," and they bring to the " cuddie ' the habits of mind of the forecastle. Therefore, while it may not be doubted that two ships were seen on an iceberg, as will he found elsewhere related, it is merely a matter of question whether these ships were those of Franklin's expedition or not? And here the Admiralty, which, up to this point, has satisfactorily performed its duty to the public, altogether fails ; for it has not furnished a single particular as to the appearance of the ships forming the unfortunate Arctic expedition. Mr. Simpson, the mate of the Renovation, describes the vessels seen by him on the iceberg as of 500 tons and of 350 tons burthen (or thereabouts) respectively ; and, as a seaman, there can be no question that he made a close approximation to the tonnage of these

ships. Were there any two of the vessels comprising the Franklin expedition of these several burthens? The Admiralty has left the public in ignorance on this point. Again, he describes the vessels upon the iceberg as painted black, with black yards, and white masts. Were those the colours of either ol Franklin's ships? Here again the public arc kept in the dark by the naval authorities. These, nevertheless, are questions that ought to be answered in the first instance ; and which, sooner or later, will compel a reply. Looking at the whole of the facts, it certainly does appear more than probable that these ships formed part of Franklin's expedition, and that this officer and

his men have perished. To suppose, as has been suggested, a region abounding in animal life, between the 75th degree and 90th degree of latitude, is a simple absurdity, seeing that from natural causes, the effects of which are obvious to all, life which cannot exist in the lower latitude cannot a priori exist in the higher. This disposes of the supposition that there may he an oasis within the Artie Circle; and, therefore, annihilates all hope of the recovery of the missing expedition. One thing, however, is certain, namely, the circumstance of the master of the Renovation having in all likelihood missed the reward offered for the discovery of Franklin. If the frozen up ships had he, n either the Erebus or Terror, that iniio idual would have been entitled to £20, OK).

An Empire founded bv a Spider. þÿ As Mahomet and his friend Abubeker sat in a dark corner of one of the caves of Thor, on the third morning after they had betaken themselves to that place of concealment, they saw their enemies ap- proach the mouth of the cavern. " What Abubeker, " it is vain to attack them, shall we do?" whispered the trembling for we are but two." " There is a third with us," said Mahomet, calmly; "God !" The pursuers, concluding from a spider's web across the opening into the recess, that no one could have recently passed in or out, withdrew, and the hidden fugitives shortly afterwards made their escape, and saved their lives. Mahomet subsequently founded an empire, which in eighty years extended its dominion over more kingdoms and countries than the Romans had subdued in eight hundred. Rut the spider that wove the cobweb was the real founder of the Mohamedan dynasty, and wrought a more extensive change in the destinies of the world than Alexander or Xerxes.

Reverence for the Sabbath. þÿ In the year 1258, at Tewkesbury, a certain Jew one Saturday fell into a cesspool, and would not allow himself to he drawn out on Saturday, on account of his reverence for the Sabbath. It seems that, our Government is about to assert and take active measures fur sustaining our exclusive right to the fisheries oi the Gulf of St. Lawrence, where American vessels, in spite of what is here understood to be the international law on the subject, are perpetually encroaching. As a means of protection,

3 T £ & © a 5£ ATI! 3< it is stated that an armed schooner is to be stationed in the Gulf. Of the inadequacy of the proposed means to effect the desired end, there need be no doubt. Still, the taking the step contemplated may prove the means of bringing the question to a definitive arbitration It is almost impossible that an armed schooner should cruise about in the Gulf of the St Lawrence with the avowed intention of protecting the fishing ground from the encroachments of American vessels without coming into collision with some of them. A broadside would doubtless result in causing the question to be brought before the Governments of England and the United States for adjustment. Beyond this, no practical result? can be expected to follow the creation of so inconsiderable a force. But it is not in the Gulf of the St. Lawrence alone that the depredations of American vessels on colonial fishing grounds are complained of ; they extend to all the fishing grounds of these Provinces Some of the Lower Provinces are far more interested than Ganada in keeping off intruders from these fisheries. The subject has often attracted a good dec I of attention in Nova Scotia, and very lately it was brought before the Legislature of the Province by the petitions of those more immediately interested in the trade. If it be true that the Americans are mere poachers on these British preserves. from which thev draw annually a revenue worth 812,000 000, it is quite time these depredations were put a stop to ; and

if they possess undoubted rights on these grounds, it is time the assertion that they are plunderers should cease to be hurled in accusation against them Along our three thousand miles of coast we do not reap more than half as much value annually from the fisheries as do the Americans, who are regarded as lawless intruders. þÿ Freedom of these fisheries was offered to the United States as part of the make-weight of that reciprocity of trade which we have so long sought to obtain from you ; and perhaps the present move of our Government may be regarded as a touch of retaliation. It is certainly for that purpose the best mode that could be adopted, far better than driving from our canals Ihe little American trade ihat we now enjoy, and refusing Americans the privilege of contributing io swell the inconsiderable revenue of our public works. It is, moreover, a thing that would meet with a far better support from the people. The increasing intimacy of our commercial connections with the U. States is evidenced in the establishment of a daily line of steamers between this city and Ogdensburg. They will no doubt create business for themselves; but it does seem almost a year too soon, seeing that the Northern Railroad is not completed þÿ Boston is awake; but perhaps she is too smart. Lundy Foot, the celebrated snuff- manufacturer, originally kept a small tobacconist's (hop at Lemenck. Ireland. One night his house, which was uninsured, was burnt to the ground. As he contemplated the smoking ruins on the following morning, in state a bordering on despair, some of the poor neighbors, groping among the embers for what they could not find, stumbled upon several canisters of unconsumed but half-baked snuff, which they tried, and found so grateful to their noses, that they loaded their waistcoat pockets with the spoil. Lundy Foot, roused from his stupor, at length imitated their example, and took a itantly struck by pinch of his own property, when he was and the superior pungency inflavor it had acquired from the great heal to which it had been exposed. Treasuring up this valuable hint, he took another house in a place called " Black-Yard," and, preparing i large oven for the purpose, set diligently about the manufacture of that high-dried commodity, which soon became widely known as " Black- Yard-Snuff;" a term subsequently corrupted into the more familiar word, " Blackguard." Lundy Foot, making his customers pay liberally through the nose for one ot the most ''distinguished" kinds of snufis in the world,

soon raised the price of his production, took a larger house in the city of Dublin, and was often heard to say. ' 1 made a very handsome fortune by being, as I supposed, utterly ruined I" Harper's Magazine, for April.

Taylor, an English author, relates in his " Records," that having restored to sight a boy who had been born blind, the lad was perpetually amusing himself with a " handglass, calling his own reflection his little man," and inquiring why he could make it do every thing he did, except to shut its byes. A French lover, making a present of a mirror to his mistress, sent with it the following lines: " This mirror my object of love will unfold, Whensoe'r your regard it allures ; Oh, would, when I'm gazing, that I might behold On its surface the object of yours !" This is verv delicate and pretty ; but the following old epigram, on the same subject, is ;n even a much finer strain : " When I revolve this evanescent state, How fleeting is its form, how short its date ; My being and my 6tay dependent still Not on my own, but on another's will : I ask myself, as I my image view, Which is the real shadow of the two ?"

Somewhat curious, if true, is an anecdote which is declared to be authentic, and which we find among the disjecta membra of our ollapodrida ; Lieutenant Montgomery had seen much military service. The wars, however, were over: and he had nothing in the world to do but to lounge about, as best he could, on his half-pay. One day he was " taking his ease in his inn," when he observed a stranger, who was evidently a foreigner, gazing intently at him. The lieutenant appeared not to notice him, but shifted his position. After short time the stranger shifted his positiou also, and still stared with unblemished, unabated gaze. This was too much for Montgomery. He rose, and approaching his scrutinizing intruder, said : ' Do you know me. sir ?" " 1 think 1 do," answered the foreigner (He was a Frenchman ) " Have we ever met before!" continued Montgomery. " 1 will not swear for it ; hot if we þÿhave and 1 am almost sure we have," said the stranger, " you have a sabre-cut, a deep one, on your right wrist." " I have," said Montgomery, turning hack his sleeve, and displaying a very broad and ugly scar. " I didn't get this for nothing, for the brave fellow who made me a present or it I repaid with a gash across his skull ' The Frenchman bent down his head, parted his hair with his hands, and said ; " You did : you may look at the receipt. The next moment they were in each other's arms. Now this story sef.ms a little problematical ; and yet it is vouched for on what ought to be considered reliable authority. In short,

In bringing before your public an article from the St. Thomas Times upon the Bill for compensation to the late owners of slaves in these Islands, it was to be hoped that you had contributed to stir the drowsiness of our community. It is now several months since every one knew the contents of the Compensation- Bill, and as yet no step has been taken and no voice raised to protest against the obvious injustice of the proposed amount of the compensation. Yet, it is our own exertions only, that we can hope to obtain the justice due to us. We have no reason to praise Count Sponneck for anything he has done for the colonies, and even the compensation he speaks of granting more in pity than in justice. The members of the Rigsdag, in stating publicly their opinions as to the merits of the case, are so far acting conscientiously for their constituents; and if some among them have arrived at wrong and unjust conclusions, it should be borne in mind, that thev have acted upon impressions formed upon scanty and often incorrect information, nay, even upon actual misrepresentations. They talk of ''force majeure þÿ for instance, as if there could be a doubt but that the insurrection would have been easily put down, if those who should have done it, had performed their duty. General Scbolten has declared on his trial, that it was in his power to quell the rebellion, but that he would not do so, in order to let the emancipation be accomplished in a way, which would debar the question of compensation. At

all events neither he, nor any other person invested with command here, did make the smallest attempt to put down the rebellion : t its outbreak, although it was reported, Count Sponneck says, by of the Fort at Western!, that every thing was ready there. If so, so much the worse, as it shews the reckless way in which our property was sacrificed and our very existence jeopardized by the Gov. General himself. But the Iligsdag, as stated, has also labored under misrepresentations, the wilest ot which, there is reason to believe, have been fabricated in this Island. There will be seen in the printed pamphlet by which I he Minister has introduced the Compensation-Bill, a document written by Mr. Arnesen, wherein he very ably refutes a series ofsilly arguments against our right to any compensation contained in a memorial sent borne from here clandestinely. By request of Government, Mr. Arnesen wrote this refutation, from which can be gleaned the amount of ignorance and perverseness, that was contained in the memorial, whose scribbler has prefered to keep himself obscure to our eyes. As the question of compensation i now the most urgent matter for us to have speedily settled, and as we mayrest assured, that if' we do not exert ourselves, we will be outdone, and may hr get nothing, may be, the trifling pittance only, proposed by the Minister, instead of the full indemnity to which we have an indisputable right, it is high time that something should be done by us. The

Rigsdag which is to assemble in Octobernext, will in all likelihood decide the matter, when doubtless fresh attempts will be made lo gain the good will of influential parties at home, by arguing away our interest, in order to promote compensation. the personal interest of the opponent find Such arguing may to ears too willing ; would we prevent it, we too must argue.

St. Thomas Times, May 20, 1852. The C olonial Law. The Colonial Law is at last a colonial galised reality. It is now in course law as the established of being le- of the land ; in other words, it is about to be recorded in the respective Courts of St. Thomas and St. John, from these to be handed over to that engine (the Press), through which only do nations or communities learn in a public sense to know what concerns or appertains to them. The Press we will then speak of in connexion with the Colonial Law and a Colonial Assembly þÿ the latter now speedily to be convened, to consider matters and things, social, religious, political, commercial, agricultural, marine and militia, in short to review, examine, and pass through the crucible every subject and circumstance, whether real or imaginary, natural or artificial. Without presuming to proclaim ourselves as yet conversant with the contents of the Colonial Law, which we believe is composed of twentysix articles, we at any rate know that the essential and especial work marked out for the Colonial Assembly is, that it shall proceed to examine clause by clause the Fundamental Law of the Imperial realm, and to debate, discuss, and finally conclude how much, how far, how little, or none at all, or all, of said respective clauses shall be found adapted, calculated or suited to the Danish West India Colonies. The Press then, in our humble bat conscientious judgment, we conceive to be that article of the law which ought first to be dealt with ; it is the fountain

þÿfront which will How thoughts, ideas, suggestions, plans, ay! objections to very other article of the Fundamental I. aw in the subsequent procedure of examination, investigation, and final adoption or rejection. The condition of the Press must then be the first subject to be decided upon, þÿ we mean particularly in a pecuniary sense, for in a political one we do not apprehend any danger, for never have we in our political course been awed by fear ! The world knows that the censorship falls feebly at the feet of the intelligent pen þÿ it has been so already, and it can be so again. The pecuniary enfranchisement of the Press in the Danish Colonies is, therefore, highly necessary, in order to give it life and vigor, and it is consequently on this point that we do hope to find the Assembly first deciding. In fact decision will be unavoidable, lor none of the present proprietors or conductors of the Danish Colonial Press will be so insane as to engage or grapple with the immense increase of public work that will be added to the present quantity, free, gratis and for nothing. The þÿ hope of reward sweetens þÿlabor, and no class of men will be found devoting their time assiduously in the exercise of public printing without proper remuneration, but that secured to them the work will be faithfully and cheerfully performed. Besides it will be the means of enlisting within the ranks of the Press both talent and respectability þÿ elements essential to make it become the organ to whose tune

high and low will be willing to sing or dance. In anticipation of these results we are now daily expecting a large addition of types and presses to our present stock, which even now is considerable, and we shall, therefore, confidingly await a liberal decision from the enlightened judgment of those who may be called by the voice of the People to preside in the Council of a Danish Colonial Parliament, for the boon and gift of which we are sincerely indebted to the liberal and generous spirit which animates and guides the actions of the Sovereign who reigns and rules over the Bealm of Denmark.

The grand military fete given by the officers of the army of Paris, and of the 1st military division, to the President, and which came oil' on Monday and Tuesday, has long absorbed all the talk. The number of persons invited exceeded 10,000, and the superficial extent occupied by the apartments was 9000 square yards. The ballroom represented a vast tent; was ornamented with military trophies ; and lighted by 24,000 wax lights It was calculated to hold more than 2000 ladies. For tiie sole benefit of die fair sex we may state that garlands and bouquets of flowers were presented to every lady oil entering, so that the ballroom presented the appearance of a beautiful flower-garden. From his tribune the President of the Republic would have a com" plete view of the whole ballroom. With regard to the þÿMonday proceedings, s we are informed that the President of the Republic left the Tuilleries about noon, attended by a brilliant cortege, composed of the marshals of France, at the head of whom rode the ex-king Jerome. The marshals were followed by the Arab chiefs, who attracted general notice, from the richness of their costume. The President arrived at the Champs de Mars at twenty minutes past twelve o'clock. He galloped in front of the troops, who were drawn up in a line, and numbered more than CO, 000 men. He then distributed the eagles to the colonels, and subsequently addressed them as follows :þÿ þÿ Soldiers, þÿ The history of nations is, in a great

measure, the iiistory of armies. On their success or reverse depends the fate of civilization and of the country. If conquered, the result is invasion and anarchy ; if victorious, it is glory and order. Thus nations, like armies, ever entertained a religious veneration for those emblems of military honour, which sum up in themselves a host of struggles and of trials. The Roman eagle adopted by the Emperor Napoleon at the commencement of this century, was the most striking signification of regeneration of the grandeur of France. It disappeared in our misfortunes ; it ought to return when France, recovered Irom her defeats, and mistress arm from the prison, he having had orders j of herself, seems not any longer to repudiate her own glory. Soldiers, resume, then, these eagles, not as s finement and convey them safely out of i tie | menace against foreign powers, but as the symbol ot and ; as the souvenir of an heroic epoch, as the sign of the nobleness of each regiproved, and Ins trial lias been out of | ment. Take again these eagles, which have so often led our fathers to victory, and swear to die in their deþÿfence. Tiie archbishop next celebrated mass, and blessed the colours, which were returned to the colonels. The troops defiled before the President, and the entire cere mony was concluded by three þÿo clock. About seventy English officers, in uniform were present. One was thrown from his horse, which hurt two priests before it was caught. The total number of troops on the ground,

and engaged in keeping order, is estimated at nearly 80,000. The correspondent of the Morning Hxrald says þÿ The fete was altogether and exclusively military. The people, probably feeling that they had little part in it, did not manifest that warmth of satisfaction which rises to enthusiasm ; yet they were pleasant and merry, and as the Prince President passed, did not fail in ottering their regards No courteous attention was paid to the press." þÿ (Ibid.,)

At 10 minutes before 3 r. m. of Thursday 6th instant, Hts Grace, the Most Revbuend Richard Patrick Smith, Archbisiio of Port of Spain, was no longer an inhabitant of this nether world. On i he last return .ol J his Grace from his pastoral tour, it was known that his health, long ago weak and suffering, had considerable declined His officiating, however, during the two principal days of the Holy week, þÿ Maundy Thursday and Good Friday, þÿ and performing divine service on Easter Sunday, produced the belief that the danger had only been transitory. But Easter Sunday was the last day on which | His Grace appeared in public ; and in the j course of the same week, he was consigned to his deathbed. As soon as the mournful circumstance became public, numbers hourly flocked to the Presbytery, still greater numbers to the Cathedral in a spirit of prayer for the | preservation of such a life. It was, however, decreed otherwise. After a severe illness of several weeks, borne with true Christian piety, and resignation, and amid the blessings | of a beloved and beloving clergy, and other persons present, life was extinct at the time above mentioned. During that day and the following, the body was embalmed, and wa3, on the night of this day conveyed in silent and solemn pomp to the Chapel of the St. George's College, where it is to lie in state,

until 8 þÿo clock of Wednesday morning. At that hour, procession w ill be formed, from a the Chapel and the corpse will be carried to the Cathedral, where the last ceremonies will be performed. Where merit is due, it must be paid, and this is our intention. Richard Patrick Smith, late Archbishop of Port of Spain, was born in the Parish of Kilbride, in the County of Cavon, Province of Ulster, in Ireland, on 17ih March 1802. We know nothing of his early youth. But as the whole of his eventful public life was spent in this island, and as we are acquainted with its extraordinary character, we may judge that the progress of youth was proportionate to that of manhood. He arrived in this colony in the year 1827 at the age of 25 years, and at a time when an unfortunate dissension existed apnong the Catholic Clergy and public of this island. First sent to the little quarter of Carenage, where the ever to be lamented Dellidder had, a short timepreviously, raised a beautiful Chapel, and formed a pious congregation, he was soon afterwards removed to the town of San Fernando. The affection which the inhabitants of that town, alter a separation of many years, still warmly expresses towards him, is evidence of the charitable and effectual manner in which he exercised his functions there. He was called to the Curacy of Port of Spain in 1834 and was consecrated Bishop of Agna on the lOilt of December 1837, by the late Right Reverend Doctor McDoncll. After the death of the latter Bishop, in November 1844, he suc-

ceeded to the title of Bishop of Olympus, and Vicar Apostolic of the British and Danish West India Islands. This new ofliee was fulfilled with so much zeal and success, and with such satisfaction to the See of Rome that by a special commission he was on the

Whatever may be the j difference of opinion respecting the degree of his merits, or talents, none can deny the peculiar abilities which within the short space j of twenty four years, with no other resouice but self, raised him from this humble station j of a poor priest, to the unprecedented dignity of Archbishop in the West Indies. AS we anticipate the time is now fast approaching for the promulgation a of the Colonial Law, and the election of Colonial Assembly, we beg to ofi'er a few remarks on this important subject. The Colonial Law, we presume, will be the foundation of the other laws, that are to follow, to regulate, the affairs of the colonies, in a moral, religious and pecuniary point of view. These laws will, ot necessity, embody trade and commerce, taxation", the relation between masters and servants, and, in short, every thing that will tend, as we sincerely hope, to ameliorate the condition and promote the happiness of the inhabitants of the d.inish westimlia Islands. Bat to ellect this desirable change, il will lie the duty of the voters to be very particular and to give their votes only in behalf of moral, intelligent and impartial men as the representatives for St. Croix in the Colonial Assembly, which, we believe, will have to report on the laws and budget for the colonies. It is to be expected that these representatives will have the welfare and happiness ot their fellowcolonists at heart, he firm and unshaken ; if not, their measures will, decidedly, tend to repudiate our rights and injure our cause; they will bear well in mind that with a shackled press the moral devi ment of a people is crushed, the dition miserable and their sentimciM itirely subdued, and that it is only through the medium of an unfettered þÿpress the organ of the people þÿ that their wrongs and injuries will be-

come known. Let us then entertain the hype that all that can lie done, will he done, and as we look forward to the coming event with no little degree ot jov and gladness, wc hail this great tavor, granted by our beloved Sovereign, token of His Majesty's paternal care as a and solicitude towards the inhabitants oi these Islands.

Turin. þÿ We find in the Piedmontese Gazette, of the 27th, an otHcial account ol the explosion of the powder manufactory at Turin, which we mentioned in our last. It took place at three-quarters past eleven a. m., at the moment when the workmen were going away. The explosion was caused by the spontaneous combustion of a mixture intended for mining powder, contained in an open vat. This was observed by two men who were on duty at the machines, and they saw the fire communicate itself to two graining cylinders which contained together 5000 kilogrammes, thence to a mixture of two thousand kilogrammes ready for graining, and, lastly, to 3000 kilogrammes spread out to dry in the open air. The explosion of this mass set fire to a small magazine containing fine gunpowder, and to another contain ing 10,000 kilogrammes of mining pow der. Meanwhile a serjeant, named Sacclii, seeing that the large magazine, containing 40,000 kilogrammes of gunpowder, was in imminent danger, boldly sprang forward, and snatched an ignited blanket away, which would undoubtedly have caused the magazine to explode, had it been left there a few seconds longer. By this time succour arrived, and the fire-engines began to play. The Duke of Genoa arrived on the spot, and gave the necessary orders. The King and the Prince de Carignan also arrived shortly after, animating the men by their presence. The number of persons killed was 14, and 21 were wounded. They were crossing the canal at the time to go to their meals, when they were over-

whelmed by the fragments which fell in all directions. At the time of the explosion the director of the manufactory, Count San Robert, was travelling by order of the Government to select a proper site at a distance from the capital to which the manufactory might be removþÿed. Ibid.

(From our own Correspondent.) TUESDAY. To-day the Champ de Mars was filled with persons who had not yet examined the decorations of the altar and tribune. W orkmen were busily engaged in finishing the arrangements for the ball that evening at the Ecole Militaire. Upwards of 20,000 persons were invited, 8000 of whom were provided with supper tickets. This was a fete offered by the army to Louis Napoleon, and it was reported that the Prince President intends to show his appreciation of the compliment by giving double pay to the army during the month of May. The subscription among the officers of the rmv of Paris for the expenses of the ball was managed in the following manner : þÿ The Commander-in-Chief gave up fifteen days' pay; Generals of Division gave up twelve days; Generals of Brigade, nine days ; Colonels, six days ; Chefs db Bataillon (corresponding to our majors), five days ; Captains, four days; and Lieutenants, two days. The ball took place in the court-yard of the Ecole Militaire which was boarded over, and formed a magnificent place for dancing, about 70 yards in length, 40 in breadth, and 27 in height. On each side of the ball-room, at a height of about six feet, two galleries had been erected, the balustrades of which were formed of infantry swords, the whole very richly decorated with groups of aims. At one end of the room was an orchestra of 800 musicians, conducted by Strauss ; at the other, a tribune had been erected for the reception of the President and the diplomatic

body. On each side of the ball-room was an ante-room, 70 yards in length and 20 in breadth; one of them was intended as a reception-room, the other for the ladies to rest in. The number of ladies present was not more than 3000, while the gentlemen numbered upwards of 16,000. Each lady on ntering the room, was presented with a oouquet. The supper- room contained twelve tables, independently of the table reserved for the President. This latter accommodated about 100 persons, while the others, which were arranged four together in three rows, held covers for upwards of 700 ladies, who retired and made way for another party of ladies, and so on until they had all supped The official programmes announced the important fact, that a reasonable time would be allowed to each parly. In other rooms refreshments had been placed for the dancers and for the suppers of the gentlemen, who supped standing, and 500 tt a time. The conversation-room was provided with two military bands; and, independently of numerous boudoirs and vestibules, there was a room where medical attendance was at hand, in case of ladies fainting, or of any of the numerous accidents peculiar to crowded ball-rooms taking place. A sufficient body of sapeurs-pommers or firemen, was present, in readiness to extinguish fire in whatever part of the building it might appear. Those who are fond of statistics, even in the hall room, will be pleased to hear that the flooring of the court-yard, contained 9000 square metres (the metre being about two
inehes longer than the English yard); that

tf, <D m <D It 2 ATll 10,000 metres of waterproof cloth were employed for the covering, that 600 metres of fir were used for the scaffolding, that 50,000 metres of drapery formed the hangings, and that 24,000 wax candles were devoted to the lighting of the whole. The service of the ball-ioom was performed by 200 iiuissiers in court dresses, while the attendance at the supper and refreshment tables was supplied by about 600 cooks, maitres d'hotee, and their employes. A leaf has been taken out of the book of our English Lord Mayor as regards the com position of the banquet, for we find the fol lowing details on the subject scattered through various journals, which announce the large supply of salmon, the enormous quantity of Bordeaux, or the prodigious number of the glasses of punch, accoiding to which appears most pleasing to the gasliotiomic mind ol the writer. The illustimus Chevet, ol the Palais Royal, sent 103 salmon, of which a latge number are said to have been trout ; he sent 103 galantines, 116 pates ol (Jhartres and Strasburg. 68 Bayonne and Westphalia hams, 18 carefully selected pates de puis oras, besides 12 " rosbtfs." There were, moreover 50 lobster mayonnaises and the same number of creams and jellies, 100 dishes of roast fowl, 100 bundles of asparagus, 216 large tarts. 744 dishes of pastry, and 444 plates of different fruits In the matter of wine there were 3800 bottles of Bordeaux, neither more nor less than 3126 bottles of champagne, 30,000 ices and sorbets, 25.000 glasses of punch, 1000 lb. of rolls and 400

loaves. When the doors of the supper room were thrown open, and the otticeis reviewed the regiments of pates, the battalions of pas try, and the brigades of ices, to say nothing of the deputations from the "armies of the land and sea" as represented by the ' rosbils' and the salmon respectively, the greatest' satisfaction is prevailed. The I'rince President arrived at ten o'clock, accompanied by the Princess Mathilda, the Matchioness of Douglas, the Marshals of France, and the Corps Diplomatique, and was received with enthusiasm. Dancing was kept up until six o'clock on Wednesday morning.

WEDNESDAY. Was the day fixed for tlie dinner given by the President, at the Palace of the Tuileries, to the commanders of the different corps and regimental deputations who were present at the distribution of the þÿeagles the Fete des Aigles, which it an pea is is to be its historical name The table at which the President sat was placed in the Salle des AJaiechaux ; the principal dignitaries of Slate were the only guests who sat with him. The other tables were arranged in the Salon d' Apollon, the Salon Blanc, and the Galerie de la Patx. It would lend to repletion were we to enumerate the dishes which composed the dinner of Wednesday, after the generous description which «ve have given of the supper of Tuesday. The fish consisted of salmon, turbot and soles. We heard of nothing in the way of meat except hams, and these were York hams, and roasted. The birds of the air were present in abundance, some of them stuffed with truffles ; and the amphibious tribes had of course been laid under contribution. Prawns, pastry, cream, French beans, straw berries, coffee and green peas, formed the less substantial pat t of the repast ; hut, as there were 800 ices and 800 demi-tasses, we presume that 800 was the number of invila

tions issued. We were surprised to find that there were sixty four plates of bon bons ; but, on the other hand, the military taste was catered for by a supply of sixty large bowls of punch. After the dinner the company of the Theatre Franqais played " Mademoiselle de la Seigliere." known to the English public as the ' Alan of Law," and " Le Rendezvous Bourgeois," frum which the quasi En glish farce of the ' Rendezvous" is taken. THURSDAY. The f£te of Thursday consisted of a display of fireworks on the high ground facing the Ecole Militaire, called the Trocadero. Every attempt was made to render it the grandest exhibition of the kind ever seen in France. It began at nine in the evening, and the signs ! for its commencement was given by the Prince President ; this was a Bengal-light, which appeared on the Ecole Militaire. The fireworks immediately commenced with a discharge of bombs and variegated stars, and eighteen cannon were at the same time fired. After the first salvo, rockets, giving forth variously coloured fires, were let off, and were succeeded by other rockets, from which blue and green flowers fell in the form rrt parachutes. Afterwards, p representation of a species of infernal combat took place. Tim infantry fired Roman candles, carrying th« most brilliant and fantastically coloured balls, in the direction of the artillery, who respond ed to this polite attention by a rolling fire ot bombes, which were discharged by 70 different mortars, and by a continuous cannonade.

After the efforts and fireworks of the soldiers had been completely exhausted, four hundred red flames burst forth from the heights of tlm Troeadero, which the imaginative were to suppose had caught fire. The displav oi fireworks concluded with n representation, in brilliant fire, of the triumphal arch in the Place du Carrousel. The pyrotechnic copy was twelve times the size of the original, and, instead of being sut mounted by a car, had a colossal eagle, with outstretched wings, soar ing over it. It bote the inscription " Viv« Louis Napoleon I" and the columns at the right and left were adorned with a gigantic cioss of the Legion of Honour, and with th« new military medal, on the same latge scale. At the same time a bouquet of bombes was fired from the largest mortars, and three lines of rockets were sent into the air. Altogether, the number of rockets fired amounted to 60,000 ! Even Thursday was not to Le the last day of these fetes, for on Friday the prefect of the Seine was to give a grand banquet to all the Generals and Colonels of the army of Paris.

DENMARK. (From the London Times," May 1 1 .) " It is a fortunate circumstance for the Earl of Malmesbury that within the short period that he has held the seals of the Foreign-office he has already had opportunity of signing a treaty with all the great Powers which restores peace to an important part of Northern Europe, secures the integrity of the Danish monarchy, and provides upon a safe basis and by an equitable compromise for the eventual succession to that Crown. But, in fact, this question had been so fully considered for the last few years, and negotiations had already been so actively carried on in all parts of Europe, that upon the arrival of M. De Bille, the Danish Plenipotentiary, in London, nothing remained to he done by the Conference but to complete its work by signing the instruments already agreed upon. This act was concluded on Saturday, the 8th of May, at the Foreign-office, and as the treaty was immediately forwarded to Copenhagen for ratification, it may now be considered that every part of this harassing controversy is brought to a close, and that the future peace of the country is secured, while the causes of past irritation and hostility are removed. For nearly six years the question of the Danish succession in the Duchies of Sclileswig and Holstein lias disturbed the tranquillity of Northern Europe, for it was in 1846 that the late King of Denmark published his letters patent on the order of inheritance in the Duchies. But the train had long before been laid

by the intrigues of the Augustenbukg family, and the explosion was greatly assisted by the convulsions which soon afterwards took place in Germany, followed by the temporary ascendancy of revolutionary principles at Frankfort and Berlin. We need scarcely remind our readers that throughout the chances and perils of this difficult period we never despaired for an instant of a cause which was supported by the whole authority of public law and defended by the spirit of the Danish people. The odds against them were overwhelming, but right has prevailed. Denmark owes her success fo no foreign Power, for throughout the contest she received no active military or naval succour. But she had the goodwill and the respect of Europe, she was upheld by public opinion, to which, we trust, we may have in some degree contributed ; and when at length Lord Palmerston was induced to lay down the principles which were established on the 2d of August, 1850, by the Protocol of London, the lights of Denmark were saved. It will he remembered that the cause of this dispute was that in the probable event of the failure of issue to the eldest male line now reigning in Denmark, the several dominions of that Crown would

pass, according to different laws of succession, and the monarchy would consequently have heen divided. Denmark Proper would have descended through a female branch to the Princess of Hesse Cassel; Holstein would have followed the strict line of male succession, because it was a fief of the German Empire ; and the succession of Schleswig was disputed, one party contending that it followed the descent of the Crown of Denmark, the other that it was indissolubly united to Holstein. To meet these dilKculties, the course which has now been successfully adopted was to select one scion of the Royal family as its common heir; to obtain renunciations of the conflicting collateral interests of all other parties, and to place the whole of these arrangements under the collective sanction of Europe. The next heir to the Crown of Denmark, in the event of the King's demise without issue, is His Majesty's uncle Ferdinand, a Prince of (id years of age, married, and likewise without issue. On his death it is presumed that the reigning line will become extinct. The present treaty, therefore, recognises as the next heir after him Prince Christian, of the line of Sonderbu rg-Gl ueks bu rg, who is married to Princess Louise ot Hesse Cassel, a granddaughter of King Frederik VI., of Denmark, by the eldest daughter of that Sovereign, who became the wife of Landgrave William of Hesse. The issue of the marriage of Prince Christian and the Princess Louise of Hesse consists of four children, the eldest a boy about 1)

years old ; and this young Prince therefore, represents both, the male and the female line of succession to the Kingdom and the Duchies, though not in the first degree. The line of Augustenburg is senior to the line of Sonderburg- Gliicksburg, but it is attainted for tiie part it took in the late contest, which was mainly lamented by those Princes in order to secure and extend their own exclusive pretensions by the dismemberment of the Danish monarchy. The Duke of Augustenburg has, therefore, forfeited Ins rights, and stands excluded from the amnesty; but an arrangement lias now, we believe, been concluded between him and the King of Denmark, by which his estates in the Duchy of .Schleswig are to be purchased at a high valuation, and the proceeds will suffice to provide liberally for his subsistence and station. No further difliculty is, therefore, to be apprehended in that quarter, and it is comparatively immaterial whether his renunciation has taken place. But the elder members of the Hessian branch had undoubted rights to the Crown of Denmark, which they have honourable renounced in favour of the husband and children of Princess Louise, without exacting any compensation. The Emperor of Russia, as representative of the line of Holstein Gottorp, had rights on one portion of the Duchy of Holstein; for the act of cession, confirmed and executed by the Grand Duke Paul, on his coming of age, in 1773, was

reigning in Denmark, and in the event ot the extinction of the male line that renunciation so made by the father of the present Emperor Nicholas would have become null and void. Far from showing any eagerness to avail himself agreed to release the Duke from the of this circumstance to acquire a preponderating influence in that part of the same, but without any claim upon Europe, it is due to the Court of Russia to state that they have never attempted to sacrifice the general welfare of the Danish monarchy to any petty interest, and that the Emperor has been constantly foremost in promoting this negotiation, of which a renewal of his father's cession of all claims on Holstein forms an essential part. Throughout this transaction Russia has acted with great

In like manner France, under the several successive Governments of Louis Philippe, Lamartine, Cavaijnac and Louis Napoleon, has pursued the same frank and consistent line of conduct towards Denmark. The difficulties came as is well known, from the sue of Germany, for this question was curiously intermingled with the political passions of the time, and the song of " Schleswig-

many months the Caira of the German revolution. At length, however, the restoration of .legitimate federal authority in Frankfort, terminated the hostilities in the Duchies; and in spite of the scorn and resentment with which our announcement of the Danish ProtDcol of 1850 was received in Germany, when the Prussian Envoy in London declined to sign that document, we have now great satisfaction in recording the fact that all differences of opinion between the great Powers have disappeared, and that Chevalier Bunsen himself has placed his name by the side of the Plenipotentiaries of all the other Powers in this final arrangement. We may therefore now invoke his high testimony to the soundness of the policy which that Protocol was intended to establish, and if any sacrifices have been made by Prussia before she arrived at this conclusion, we sincerely hope she may be rewarded for them by the establishment of a cordial alliance between herself and Denj mark, whose geographical position and maritime power make her a neighbour of the utmost value to the Prussian dominions. Upon the whole, this treaty is another proof that in spite of the most serious obstacles and the most viplent passions, the active, intelligent and pacific diplomacy ot our day does contrive to avert the calamities of general war, and even when hostilities are raging, to confine them, as far as possible, within a narrow compass. In any other age, it is highly probable that the Danish struggle would have led to far more formidable

results; and although it was too long protracted because vigorous means were not early employed to check it, the termination of the whole negotiation proves that the great Powers will see justice done and peace preserved. When the new ocean mail contracts into which the Government has recently entered come into operation, the whole cost to the nation for conveying its sea-borne correspondence will amount to nearly a million sterling per annum. The ocean mail packet lines served by this country will then be about 60,000 miles in length ; and the number of miles which the British mail packets will traverse annually will be nearly 2,500,- 000. The number of letters which these packets will carry in the course of a year, at the present postal packet rates, will be about thirty millions. The relative importance of different parts of the wot Id with this country may be estimated by the frequency of the mail packet communication with them. Thus, the communication with Trance will be twice daily ; with Belgium, once daily ; with Holland and Hamburg, twice weekly ; with America, weekly; with the East Indies and tho IV ninsula, three times monthly; with the Cape of Good Hope, five times every two months ; with the West Indies, China, the west coast of Africa, Central America, Chili, Peru, and the Spanish Main, twice monthly ; and with Australia, Brazil, Mexico, and Buenos Ayres, monthly. The principal steam packet companies who have contracts with the Government are, the Pacific, the British and American, the West India, and the Peninsular and Oriental Companies. The Pacific steam Navigation Company has hitherto confined its operations to the south western coast of America, between Panama and Valparaiso. It will most pro-

bably extend its enterprise to California, and materially assist in the navigation of the Pacific Ocean, and in establishing a western communication with Australia. The British and American Steam Packet Company is distinguished for the success with which it has navigated the North Atlantic Ocean. It has been in advance of all the other steam packet companies, as far as the perfection of its vessels is concerned ; and in taking immediate advantage of every discovery in the improvement of steamers. Its shipbuilding career has been one continued tnumph, each of its packets having surpassed its predecessor in magnitude and speed. The operations of this company have consisted almost exclusively in running packets between England and the United States, and British North America. When California was discovered, it was expected that the British and American Company would have extended its enterprise southward from New York, in eider to share the immense traffic that would arise on that route. It has not, however, seen fit to do so, and has allowed the American people to monopolise the whole of the sea traffic between New York and San Francisco. The iloyal West India Mail Packet Company differs from all other companies in having commenced its existence as a great company, and in undertaking at the outset of iis career a vast and magnificent ocean mailpacket scheme. It has been more unfortunate than all the other companies together, having lost, in the space of ten years, a splen-
did fleet of iteamcrs, the destruction of which

T, ® R © I ATI S3 has caused some of the most terrible and heart-rending calamities recorded in the history «f ocean navigation. It is singular that from the first mail-packet scheme, projected by ths company, there would seem to have been anticipated some great discovery in the Pacifc in connexion with the United States, since it comprehended a communication between the Darien Gulf and New York. It is curioas to observe, also, the changes which this company's mail route scheme has undergone. In the first instance, of so little importance were the North and South American ports in the Pacific considered that Ohagres was never visited until the northern Antiles had been served, and then only by a branch steamer, once a month, from Jamaica. As for Grey Town, it was not even mentioned in their scheme Now, however, there is a direct communication between England, and Ghagres, and Grey Town, once every fourteen days. The gn at policy ol the Boyal Mail Company, at present, is to prevent the riches and traffic, originating on the eastern shores of the Pacific, from passing to this countrv bv wav of New York; and to diaw it to England, by a direct north-easterly course, from the isthmus of Panama To accomplish this, gigantic steamers are running between St. Thomas and their home station ; the number of inter-colonial packets of the company is to be augmented, and its trade with Mexico to be partially sacrificed. The Peninsular and Oriental Company was the most insignificant of all the packet com-

panies, and has become the greatest of any. It first possessed, as a foreign packet company, two or three steamers only, which were employed in coasting in the Bay of Biscay, and it now possesses a fleet of which a nation might be proud. In a few months its fleet will consist of upwards of thirty steamers, which will cover a sea and ocean line 15 000 miles in length. The operations of this company have been spreading eastward with marvellous rapidity. The company has now secured the principal traffic of the eastern world, which w ill scarcely be interfered with, even when a western communication with Australia is established Trading with the richest and most populous countries on the globe, with no great ocean to cross, have made the Peninsular and Oriental Company the wealthiest and most fortunate steam packet company in the world. The Mail steam packet service of this country is one of its growing achievements, and will leave more lasting and beneficial traces of its greatness than any monument existing of the most celebrated nations of antiquity ; for by its agency the English name and language will be extended over the civilised world, and the fame of England will rest on commerce and not on conquest. There can be little doubt that if a uniform foreign postal rate, sufficiently low in amount, prepaid by stamps, were substituted for the present charges, the oversea correspondence of this country would probably increase fiom 30 millions of letters a year to 300 millions,

without any additional expense to the government. In consequence of the introduction of penny postage the inland correspondence of this country increased from 90 millions of letters a year to 400 millions. If increased facilities for trade and commerce had not arisen in the country a few years since, the penny postage could not have caused such an increase in the number of letters; and even if it had, no meant would have existed

4 for its conveyance without the assistance of railroads. Thus the cause of increase afforded facilities for its existence. In like manner the extension of railway and steam navigation all over the world increases foreign trade and international intercourse, and this extension would cause a vast addition of out foreign correspondence, and would afford the requisite facilities for its conveyance and existence. It is the peculiar privilege of England to be the ocean mail carriers for almost the whole world. Her mail packet system, extends, in Europe and Africa, from Hamburg to the Cape of Good Hope ; in America, from Halifax to the Uiver Plate ; and from the Panama Gulf to the southermost limit of Chili; and in it is comprehended the whole of the sea coast of Asia. The Dutch and the Spaniards are indebted to her for carrying their mails to and from Java and the Philippines; and she carries the correspondence of every maritime power in Europe which has dependencies in the west. Her power to do good by means of cheap foreign postage is enormous By it she could materially advance civilisation, encourage international peace and amity, assist emigration, and augment the commerce of the world. By refusing to bestow the boon of cheap foreign postage, she will neglect her high mission, and incur an unenviable responsibility. No one who has ever seen a foreign mail arrive at or leave this country could fail to have been struck with the ludicrous disproportion existing between its bulk, the magnitude of

the steamers appointed to carry it, and the enormous sums paid to the packet companies for its conveyance ; and yet this mail contains literally the seaborne correspondence o! one portion of the world wiih the other. Great Britain, by acting generously, and reducing her high packet rates of postage, may claim the homage and the gratitude of all nations; but by keeping up her impolitic charges and contracting international correspondence within nairnw limits she will deservedly incur their censure.

Truth in 1'leasure, þÿ Men have been said to be sincere in their pleasures, but this is only that the tastes and habits of men are more easily discernible in pleasure than in business ; the want of truth is as great a hindrance to the one as to the other. Indeed, there is so much insincerity and formality in the pleasurable department of human life, especially in social pleasures, that instead of a bloom there is a slime upon it, which deadens and corrupts the thing. One of the most comical sights to superior beings must be to see two human creatures with elaborate speech and gestures making each other exquisitely uncomfortable from civility ; the one pressing what he is most anxious that the other should not accept, and the other accepting only from the fear of giving offence by refusal. There is an element of charity in all this too ; and it will he the business of a just and refined nature to be sincere and considerate at the same time. This will be better done by enlarging our sympathy, so that more things and people are pleasant to ns, than by increasing the civil and conventional part of our nature, so that wc arc able to do mure seeming with greater skill and endurance. þÿ 1'rifnps in Council.

Till Snowy Mountains in New Zealand. þÿ The " Wellington Independent" gives the following account of a recent expedition made by the Lieutenant-Governor to the Middle Island: After leaving the Wairau, having traversed the Kaparatehau district, his Excellency and his attendants reached the snowy mountains to the southward, about four short days' journey from the Wairau, and encamped at the foot of the 1 apuenukomountain, which they ascended. Previously to starting into the pass which is supposed to exist between the Wairau and Port Cooper plains, his Excellency ascended the great snowy mountain which forms the principal

peal of the Kaikoras, and which attains an elevation ot at least 9000 feet, the upper part being heavily covered with snow to a great depth. He succeeded in reaching the top of the mountain, but so late as to be unable to push on to the southern edge of the summit, when an extensive view southwards would have been obtained. In returning, a steep face of the hill (little less than perpendicular), down which hung a bed of frozen snow, had to be crossed for a considerable distance. Mr. Eyre, who had led the party up the dangerous ascent, was in advance with one native the others being 200 feet before and behind him, on the same perpendicular of the snow. He heard a cry, and looking round, saw Wiremu Hoeta falling down the precipice, pitching from ledge to ledge, and rolling over and over in the intervals, till he fell dead, and no doubt smashed to pieces at a depth below of about 1500 feet, where his body could be seen in a sort of ravine, but where it was impossible to get at it. His Excellency narrowly escaped from similar destruction, having lost both feet from under him, and only saving himself by the use of an iron-shot pole which he carried. Another of the natives had a still narrower escape, having actually fallen about fifteen yards, when he succeeded in clutching a rock and saving himself. The gloom which this unfortunate event caused, and the uncertainty of crossing the rivers while the snows are melting, induced his Excellency to return.

Escape of Cuban Prisoners. þÿ The Liverpool Courier of the 5th inst., announces the escape of Major Schlessinger, Colonel Alego Iznaga, Mr. Juan O'Rourke, and Mr. J. B. Perez and other Cuban prisoners from the Spanish penal colony of Ceuta, in Africa, and their arrival in Liverpool on the 3d. tnst. Schlessinger and such of his associates as were not Americans or English were sentenced by the Spanish Government to ten years' hard labor in chains in Ceutn, where thev were subjected to great hardship and suffering. After their escape from the fortress in which they were confined, they made their way to Gibraltar, where they got on board the steamship Genoa for Liverpool. It is their intention to leave England as soon as possible for this country, where they will doubtless receive a hearty welcome from their friends. New York Journal of Commerce, May 19.

Our Trade with Denmark. þÿ The new Cabinet in London excites considerable alarm in Denmark. The immense commercial activity which has sprung up between the two countries since the establishment of free trade would at once disappear if this system were endangered. The exports of Denmark þÿ corn, cattle, dairy produce, &c þÿ, cannot bear any higher duty than that they now pay. The Danish peasant now feeds many thousands of our British handicrafts-men, and buys their production in return. Lord Derby will entirely ruin this mutually beneficial trade by reimposing the hateful taxes on the food of the people. Quick passage of an American Clipper Ship from China A large American clipper-built ship, the " Witch of the Wave," Captain Millett, commander, has recently arrived in the East India Docks. London, from Canton, having made one of the most extraordinary and rapid voyages on record. She has also brought one of the most valuable cargoes of Tea that perhaps ever entered the Port of London, having on board no fewer than 19,000 chests of the choicest quality. She is nearly 1,400 tons burden, the size of our largest lndiamen, and was built at Salem, near New York, in tho course of last year. She proceeded to California, thence to Hong Kong,

>0 ® b U £ A 'T 113. and sailed from Whampoa, near Canton, on the 5th January : made the passage to Javahead in 7 days and 12 hours, then had the wind W. S W. to N. W. for several days, with light trade-wind, and made the Cape in 29 days. Then encountered strong easterly winds from the Western Islands, and took a pilot off the Dungeness on the 4th of April, making a passage from China to the Downs in 90 days, a trip surpassing the celebrated runs of the Oriental and Surprise American clippers. Had she not encountered ihe strong easterly winds up the Channel, she would have accomplished the voyage several days earlier. As it was, she was only four days beating up from the Chops of the Channel to reaching the River while some of oui large vessels were nearly a fortnight doing the distance. The Witch of the Wave is the object of much interest as she lies in the docks. Her bows are similar to those of a largesized cutter yacht. By the above it will be seen that she sailed round the world in ten months and a half, including loading and discharging at the above ports. The greatest distance she ran in 24 hours on the voyage to London was 338 miles

Kossuth's Family. þÿ It having been found impossible to establish a case against Mesdames Meszlenyi and Ruttkay, they have been liberated, and are now residing in the Hotel National, in the Leopoldstadt- The Austrian Government has at length come to the conclusion that nothing is to be gained by detaining Kossuth's relations here, and occordingly the whole family þÿ some 17 persons, I believe þÿ will be permitted to quit this country on the 1st of May. As people here can never do anything with a good grace, difficulties have been raised about the servants who were willing to go with the emigrants The authorities insist on the Kossuth family emigrating alone, which in my opinion is most unreasonable, as there aie four females and eleven children of the party. From a perfect credible source 1 learn that Madame Meszlenyi, who is said to have as much moral courage as all the rest of her family put together, completely baffled all the attempts of the authorities to extract any information of consequence from her. The military judge (auditor), to whom the case was intrusted, dictated to a protocol purporting to be a recapitulation of the admissions made by the defendants, and Madame Meszlenyi was instructed to sign it. "Never" cried the spirited woman, " will 1 consent to sign that which, though not positively false, is not perfectly true. Let me dictate the

protocol, which 1 am well able to do, and then 1 will willingly sign it." Justice requires that I should state that Kossuth's sisters were kindly treated during their imprisonment and that their mother's letters to them were duly delivered after having been read by the authorities to whose safe keeping they were entrusted. The old lady admonished her children to take courage and to remain firm, "as the sun must rise at last, be the night ever so dark and long." This, I have reason to believe, is the sense, if not the literal translation, of a phrase contained in one of lbs letters delivered into the hands of the prisoners. As Madame Kossuth and her family will not be permitted to come here, they will meet with Mesdaines Meszlenyi and Ruttkay somewhere on the road to Bodenbach. [Vienna Correspondent of the Times.

A Tiger Story þÿ The following remarkable escape has been mentioned in private letters by the last mail from India. Two young officers, Lieut. Hugh Elliot, of the Bombay cavalry, son of Capt. Charles Elliot, Governor of Bermuda, and Lieut. Rice, ol the 25th, were out shooting, when they fell in with a tigress and two cubs. One cub was immediately killed, and the tigress wounded. They trarked her for half an hour into the jungle, when she suddenly sprang out, knocked over Mr. Elliot before he had time to cock his gun, and, seizing him by lb# arm, dragged him away. Mr Rice had already discharged one gun when they attacked the tigress. He quickly got his second gun, but, from the extreme difficulty ol firing without killing his friend, could only aim at the body of the tigress and though h« wounded her again, did not wound her mortally. With admirable resolution he ihcu seized a third gun, and, watching his opportunity till he could see Elliot's head apart from that of the tig i ess, shot her dead through the head, with his friend in her mouth. The officers were thirty miles from camp, and did not reach it for twenty hours. It is impossible to give too much credit to the skiff and coolness of Lieut. Rice. Mr Elliott's arm is badly wounded by the bite, as well as by the stones and rocks over which he wus dragged, but no fear is entertained for his life or bit limb.

TRANSLATION. Under date of 26th March this year the following COLONIAL LAW Fob the Danish West India Possessions has been issued through the Ministry of Finances : WE FREDERIK the SEVENTH, by the Grace of God King of Denmark, of the Vandals and Goths, Duke of Sleswick, Holstein, Stormarn, Ditmarsh, Lauenburg and Oldenburg. Make known: The Diet has passed and we have sanctioned the following law : I. 1. There shall be erected for the Danish West India Possessions a Colonial Assembly, invested, in thq manner ordained hereafter, with a deliberative voice with regard to the exercise of the legislative power. On the motion of the Colonial Assembly the King may decree its division into two Assemblies, the one for St. Croix and the other for St. Thomas and St. Johns, for the transaction of all business or of some particular branches and make the provisions, required bv this alteration in the present law. $ 2. It pertains to the King, after having received the report of the Colonial Assembly, to enact, on the responsibility of the respective Minister, as prescribed by the fundamental law of the realm, ordinances, relative to : 1) the extension of the general laws of Denmark to the Danish West India Islands ; 2) the municipal affairs of the Islands, including schools and public instruction, the support of the poor, the militia, the road department, fences and trespasses, the relations between employers and labourers, masters and servants, vagrancy, the public health, the fire department, and

the executive police on the whole. The ordinances under 1) may contain deviations from the laws in force in the Mother Country, if the local peculiarities of the colonies should particularly require them, but such modifications cannot affect the principles of the laws. Laws thus modified are as soon as possible to be laid on the table of the Diet together with the report of the Colonial Assembly on the subject. The Colonial Assembly has also, without being called upon by the Government, the right of expressing its opinion with regard to the application of all laws and ordinances for Denmark in the colonies, and its report shall in such cases likewise be laid on the table of the Diet. The legislative power thus placed in the King, cannot however, be any impediment to the passing of laws, respecting also such mat- ters as are treated of in this , if the King and Diet agree thereon tn the usual manner. $ 3 With regard to all other matters, not mentioned in 2, the legislative power is exercised by the King and Diet conjointly. But, unless very particular reasons should render an exception necessary, the report of the Colonial Assembly on the subject shall always be received, before any law can be passed for the Danish West India Possessions. The Colonial Assembly shall likewise be given a timely opportunity of expressing itv opinion upon that part of the Budget,

AT3I which relates to the West India possessions, so that, unless circumstances have rendered it impossible, the report of the Colonial Assembly must alwavs " be previously produced. 4. In particularly urgent cases the Governor is authorized to issue provisional regulations relative to such matters, as are adapted to proceedings in conformity with 2 and 3. The matter is then legally proceeded with in the next meeting of the Colonial Assembly and as far as it requires to be decided, in conformity wiih 3 the Government shall lay the same before the Diet in its first session, to be proceeded with in the manner prescribed for provisional laws, or in case the Colonial Assembly should not have finished at that time its deliberations on the subject, in the second session of the Diet, after the publication of the regulation in question. 5. Whenever the Colonial Assembly may deem a change in the laws or institutions of the Islands, desirable, or whenever it may think to have cause of complaint, on account of the manner, in which the laws are administered or the institutions managed, it is authorized to address the Governor in writing on such matters, or to transmit to this functionary its representations to the King But the petitions and complaints of private individuals ought to be referred to the King or the proper authorities, unless a member of the assembly adopts such a representation as his own. G. It pertains to the Colonial Assembly to cause the revision ol all municipal accounts

and the fimil decision, relative to them, rests likewise with the assembly. An extract of these accounts shall be published and a copy of this extract transmitted to the Governor. II. 5 7. The Colonial Assembly consists of 16 members, elected by the people, viz: 8 for St. Croix, G for St. Thomas arid 2 for St. Johns, and of 4 members, appointed by the King. 8. The Island of St Croix is divided into 2 elective districis, formed by the border-lines between the jurisdictions of Christiansted and Frederiksted, so that the former jurisdiction elects 5 and the latter 3 members. The two other Islands form each one elective district. The members are elected for the term of 4 years The half of the elected members withdraw every second year, the first time by drawing lots For Christiansteds jurisdiction withdraw the first time 3 for that of Frederiksied 1, for St. Thomas 3 and for St. Johns 1 member, but they may be le-eler.ted The half of the membeis appointed by the King, withdraw likewise every second year and may also be re-elected $ 9. The franchise or tight of voting is vested in every male of unblemished character, who is a native or has resided in the Islands for 5 years, when he is 25 years old and has not been legally deprived of the management of his property, and either has a yearly income of ®500 or pays an annual amount of at least 85 in ground and building tax to the State. He must, moreover, have resided a year within the district, in which he sojourns at the time the election takes place.
$ to. Eligible as a member of the Colonial Assembly is every person, who possesses the

qualifications required for the exercise of the elective franchise. But a person eligible in other respects may be elected, even if his settled place of abode is not within the district. $ 11. It is the duty of the judges in the 3 towns and of the judge of St. Johns to superintend, each in his district, the poll as Director. The Governor causes, through the medium of the respective Burgher Council, annually an alphabetical list to be made out of all persons in the elective district, who are entitled to vote, with full information with regard to their names, age, vocation and abodes. i 12. The list thus made out is to be exhibited a fortnight in a proper place for public examination, and is this to be made publicly known with at least 8 days' notice. $ 13. Should the name of any person, who does not possess the qualifications, which entitle to vote, be found on the list, or any person wrongly be omitted in the same, any one may give notice in writing thereof to the superintendent of the poll and produce the necessary evidence at least 3 days previous to the election, and the superintendent shall summon not only the person, to whom the notice refers and to whom he shall hand a copy of the same, but also the person by whom the objection has been made. $ 14, The day as well as the place of election is to be fixed by the Governor and the elections shall take place on the same day in all the districts The superintendents of the poii have then, in the usual manner, to give pub-

lic notice, at least 4 days previous to the same, of the place, in which the election is to be held, and of the day arid hour, when it is to commence. 15. Each superintendent employs two respectable persons, well known in the district, as assistants, and after having called their attention to the importance of the trust committed to them, allots to each his employment. $ 16. The superintendent of the poll and his assistants are to meet at the election, on th« day and hour appointed, and bring with them the lists for the whole district and the objections made to them, if any such have been made. The superintendent opens the proceedings and takes care that the elections are proceeded with in the best possible order. Previous to the commencement of the poll the superintendent has to decide the objections made to the lists, and his decisions are to l>s entered iu the protocol of proceedings. 17. Thereafter the election is to be proceeded with, under the direction of the superintendent. Every person, who will exercise his right of voting, must meet in person at the place, where the election is to he held. When such peison comes forward for the purpose ot voting, he names as many persons as there are to be elected members for his district (paragraph 8), adding also their full names, rank, vocations and abodes. The votes are to he registered in two protocols, of which each assistant of the superintendent keeps one, so that in the one are entered the name of each voter and at the side thereof the
names of the persons, for whom he has voted, but in the other the names of the persons

elected, and under each name those of the voters The entries are to he read to the elector, to be vended by him and compared with each other, $ 18. When no more persons offer their votes at the election the superintendent and the assistants enter their own votes. After the close of the poll, the votes for each person elected are to be counted and the result made known to the presons present. The persons, that have received the greatest number of votes, are declared the representatives of the district. In case that two or more persons have an equal number of votes, the election is to be decided hv drawing lots. 19 Those who have been elected are to receive notice in writing of their election from the superintendent of the poll and are at the same time to be requested to declare, if they accept the election Functionaries require no special permission to accept the same.
