St. Thomas Times, June 12, 1852. The Tied way's News. The II. M. Company's ship Meduay arrived here at 6 o'clock this morning. She left Southampton on the afternoon ol the 26th ultimo. The Parana arrived home at 8 p. m., on the 22nd. " All well on board." The political news by the Meduay may be summed up in the following items. In the House of Lords, on the 24th of ALay, the Eari. of Derby delivered a very impressive speech in favor of extending protection to the British West India Colonies, which had been replied to by the ex-Colonial Secretary (Earl Grey), who in the language of the Daily Neus, had driven the Premier into a corner of the House, by his masterly defence of free-trade in sugar. Lord Palmf.rston had made a crack speech in the Commons, wherein he depicted the dangers to be apprehended for all constitutional liberty in Europe, and concluded by charging the British Cabinet with coquetting with Prince Louis Napoleon. The English Militia Bill had fairly passed through committee, andasamended by that process, had been placed in print before the public, and would in a few weeks most likely become the law of England. Prince Louis Napoleon remains firm at his post as head of France þÿ his power and popularity appearing to depend upon the continuation of extensive daily fetes, þÿ which he insists upon the members of the Cabinet to celebrate, if even at the cost of the public moneys, þÿ and the splendid military displays which go on from day to day. The Emperor Nicholas still continued to be a guest of the King of Prussia :

and immense military reviews occurred in Berlin daily. The Emperor takes great pains to flatter the Prussian military, and to strengthen their dislike to civilians. The Austrian Government is again in the English market, endeavouring to raise a loan of £3, 000, 000 sterling.

The household Jewels. A TRAVELER, from journeying In countries far away, Repassed his threshold at the close Of one calm Sabbath day ; A voice of love, a comely face, A kiss of chaste delight, Were the first things to welcome him On that blessed Sabbath night.

He stretched his limbs upon the hearth. Before its friendly blaze, And conjured up mixed memories Of gay and gloomy days ; And felt that none of gentle soul However far he roam, Can e'er forego, can e'er forget, The quiet joys of home,

" Bring me my children!" cried the sire, With eager, earnest tone ; " I long to press them, and to mark IIow lovely they have grown; Twelve weary months have passed awa» Since I went o'er the sea, To feel how sad and lone I was Without my babes and thee."

Refresh thee, as 'tis needful," sard The fair and faithful wife, The while her pensive features paled. And stirred with inward strife ; " Refresh thee, husband of my heart I ask it as a boon Oux children are reposing, love ; Thou shalt behold them soon."

She spread the meal, she filled the cup. She pressed him to partake ; He sat down blithely at the board, And all for her sweet sake ; But when the frugal feast was done The thankful prayer preferred. Again affection's fountain flowed ; Again its voice was heard.

" Bring me my children, darling wife. I'm in an ardent mood ; My soul lacks purer aliment, I long for other food ; Bring forth my children to my gaze Or ere I rage or weep, I yearn to kiss their happy eyes Before the hour of sleep."

' I have a question yet to ask ; Be patient, husband dear A stranger, one auspicious morn. Did send some jewels here ; Until to take them from my care. But yesterday he came, And I restored them with a sigh þÿ Dost thou approve or blame >"

I marvel much, sweet wife, that thou Shouldst breathe bhcIi words to mc Restore to man, resign to God, Whate'er is lent to thee ; Restore it with a willing hearl. Be grateful for the trust ; Whate'er may tempt or try us. wife, Let us be ever just."

She took him by the passive hand, And up the moonlit stair, She led him to their bridal bed, With mute and mournful air ; She turned the cover down, and there, In grave-like garments dressed. Lay the twin children of their love, In death's serenest rest.

" These were the jewels lent to mc, Which God has deigned to own ; The precious caskets still remain, But, ah, the gems are flown ; But thou didst teach mc to resign What God alone can claim ; Me giveth and he takes away. Blest be His holy name !"

3 ir <& m © II AT i s, The father gazed upon his babes, The mother drooped apart, While all the woman's sorrow gushed Prom her o'erburdened heart ; And with the strivinjof her grief, Which wrung the tears she shed Were mingled low and loving words To the unconscious dead.

When the said sire had looked his fill, He vailed each breathless face, And down in self-abasement bowed, For comfort and for grace; With the deep eloquence of woe Poured forth his secret soul, Rose up, and stood erect and calm, In spirit healed and whole.

"Restrain thy tears, poor wife," he said, " I learn this lesson still, God gives, and God can take away, Blest be His holy will ! Blest are my chiidren, for they live From sin and sorrow free, And I am not all joyless, wife, With faith, hope, love, and thee."

The following is thn letter : þÿ Mormon Bar, North Fork of the American River þÿ Sunday, May 2, þÿ1852. The excitement in regard to the Chinese is rapidly extending along the banks of the North Fork of the American River, and daily expulsions are taking place. This morning some sixty Americans ranged down the river some four milei, driving off two hundred, quietly removing their tents, strictly respecting their persons and property ; except in one instance, when a Celestial seemed inclined to be þÿ obstreperous, his cradle was thrown into tin river. The same company intend to proceed en mass to Horse Shoe Bar this afternoon, to concert measure with the miners there to þÿ þÿstart some four hundred located at that place. A band of music is engaged to accompany the expedition. The feeling is strong, and anything but evanescent, that self-protection, as a first law- of nature, must and shall be enforced. Would it not be well for your city government to take some action on the subject, for you will certainly have a flood of them from above and below you soon. There is but one opinion among the miners in regard to the proposed monopolies and importation of Chinese into the mines, and nearly all of the eighty or ninety thousand American miners are fully determined to submit no longer to have the public lands robbed of their only treasure. It appears that the excitement was rapidly increasing, and that about 20,000 people had already reached the place from the neighbouring colonies. Special instances were mentioned in which parties had obtained gold valued at about £30 per day for several successive days, while even since the scarcity of water the average at the chief point of operation had been £3. These results were principally obtained from surface diggings on a slope of the range not a quarter of an acre in extent. It was estimated that since the discovery the general yield, including what had found its way into the banks, had been at least £1,000,000 sterling, and that already, up to the 18th of January, £660,000 had been exported to this country. When the winter rains should set in, it was anticipated that the most extraordinary consequences would lie witnessed. In the meantime labour

was fetching high rates; reapers were paid 28s. a-day, besides a considerable allowance of spirits, and servants who previously obtained about £30 to £35 per annum were now readily engaged at £60. The retail business of the place had improved in proportion, the expenditure by the mining population being distinguished for its extravagance. The latest price of gold was £2 18s. to £3 per ounce. But besides a similar Dill may he brought forward in the coming session of the Rigsdag, as the principal objection to the last was inexpediency, the absurd and indelicate reflections made by those members on the Colonists in general, are circumstances, which forbid us to place the decision of our future destiny perhaps in the hands of such men. When we see grave legislators unscrupulously asserting, and others patiently listening to their assertions, that the Colonies are merely merchandize to he disposed of to the highest bidder, and that 40,000 fellow-citizens, without regard to their predilections or well-being, without being consulted, can he transferred like cattle, we will not say like slaves, for even these were permitted to choose masters, from one owner to another; we are certainly justified in regretting, that in conformity with the 3 of the Colonial Law the legislature of the Mother Country can now uncontrolled legislate for the inhabitants of these islands. While we find that in II $9 of the Colonial Law one class of citizens (burghers,) who have always hitherto exercised Hie elective franchise, the continua-

tion ot which was promised to them in the original draft, has been disfranchised, we discover that ground and building-tax to the State Treasury only qualifies the elector. That municipal taxes do not entitle the payer thereof even to vote for members to serve in the Colonial Assembly, is somewhat astonishing, when we reflect, that the power of this Board is confined to matters, which may be strictly termed municipal. But the astonishment becomes greater, when we remember, that, although those, who do not pay any tax whatever, we allude to per sons possessing an income of $500 or above, are eligible as members of the Council, tax-payers to the State Treasury are excluded from exercising the fra n chise, namely such as pay a fraction less than $5 tax, and do not enjoy an income of $500, withal they may lie burghers. Besides there is another class of citizens (Rumshop keepers) who, notw ithstand mg they pay a considerable tax to the State Treasury, can only exercise the franchise, if they possess an income of | 8500. That the $27 of the 4th section of the original draft has been omitted in the Colonial Act, is certainly to he regretted ; for sound policy imperatively demands, that all officers exercising the executive and judicial functions in the colonies ought not to be permitted to own landed property in these islands, as they may under such circumstances be looked on as parties interested. For Hie St. Croix 4vis ! It is a notion generally entertained bv many persons in this community, that the natives have to thank the foreigners established here, for the prosperity of tliis Island, or in other words its happy situation and laws do not contribute to its well-being. We allow, that at first sight the idea may be admitted, but on maturely reflecting on the matter, we will certainly find it erroneous and absurd in the highest degree. It is an incontrovertible fact, that a man on leaving his native land, for the purpose of acquiring a fortune, will proceed to that place, where he will be able in the shortest space of time to do so. If the preference is given to St. Thomas by those who arrive here with a small capital, it is therefore owing to the advantages, which this Island yields them to obtain their object. No rational being will suppose, that such men quit their homes, parents, relations, and connexions, taking frequently their all, in the puerile intention of enriching the natives. It is a matter of necessity, not of choice with them. St. þÿThomas s, from its geographical position, affords facilities, of which none of the other Antilles can boast. The same cause which makes it the direct place of arrival and departure of the leviathan British Steamers makes it the vast emporium of the wide world. As much as it would he ridiculous to believe that John Bull gives us the preference over her innumerable possessions in the Carribean seas merely to favor us,

so would it betray share ignorance to assert, that any foreigner establishes himself here to benefit the Island. The duties levied here on goods imported are inconsiderable, and yet they are not paid by the merchants, for they are added to the costs, and the consumers here and the purchasers from abroad consequently pay the duties. No direct taxes to the State are imposed on the merchants. To the Country Treasury they contribute in the Store Tax. But while many House Owners, whose properties yield an insignificant revenue in comparison to the gains of the merchants, pay higher rates to the Island Treasury, the Store Tax even of the 1st class is entirely disproportionate to the Rumshop and other Trade Taxes to said Treasury. In St. þÿT.iomas sthe merchant can at night retire to rest with safety; Ins repose is not disturbed by the fear of internal commotions or external invasions. There is no dread of þÿ Esperas, and other delays of the law. lie is freely permitted to import as many clerks as he likes to the detriment of the natives. 'There is no let or hindrance to his landing or shipping his goods at or from auv place in the harbor, no þÿ searchers anil þÿwaiters. Through the British postal arrangements he in advance of all other merchants in this part of the world receives the first intelligence of the ni ,rkets in the other parts ol the globe. But why multiply instances, when the fact is so very evident, from Ins fixing his abode among us? ft may be asked if St. Thomas derives

no benefit whatever from those foreigners. We are far from denying it, we admit that we owe something to them, but we assert that they all owe us more. What we contend is, that we need not entertain the absurd notion, that, if we do not allow them to ride rough-shod over us, they will abandon St. Thomas. Whatever they may say, believe me, sir, they are too wise, not to know, that the vacancies would soon be filled up by their more judicious countrymen. St. Thomas, 22d June 1852. T. O.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Arit. Sir, It is with a great deal of pleasure that I hail the sp pearance of tlio 1st number of the Official Gazette " The plan I highly approve of, but I am sorry that I ( cannot say as much regarding the translation or English I part of this paper. I hope we will, for the future, be furnished with translations more in accordance with th« rules of English composition. Not only is the translation, in many places, far from a strict accordance with the original ; but the rules of construction and arrangement are in a great measure violated, The 12th as it stands in this Gazette is completely in the form of an interrogation. It only requires a note of interrogation to set it off to admiration. I give it hero with tins addition : ) 12. þÿ The list thus made out is to be exhibited a fortnight in a proper place for public examination, and is this to be made' publicly known with at least 8 days' notice þÿ? But now, I will take this opportunity to say a few words on tlie Law itself. A good deal of indifference to this Law, I am sorry to see, prevails in the community. People have, considering the expectation which had been raised by the masterly production of the Committee, appointed to report on the Draft, been disappointed to some extent. It is quite true, that the present Law differs in so many respects from the advise of this Committee, that the Diet, in its superior wisdom, might well have dispensed with the labour of these men. Still, I cannot

conceive, why many of the town-inhabitants, as report says, should, from displeasure or indifference, refuse to give up themselves as qualified to vote. This act alone, I consider a sufficient proof, that these persons ARE IN REALITY NOT QUALIFIED TO VOTE. Instead of trying their utmost to elect as members of this Council, a couple, at least, of men who would advocate the interest of the towns-people, they by refusing to vote, will be left entirely without a voice in the conduct of affairs, which I am afraid will be altogether in the hands of the Planters. The natives especially, should take more interest in. and make the best of, this law. We cannot expect the Foreigners among us to do so. They did not com here for that ; and they, 1 suspect, would care very little whether we had on our backs a Louis Napoleon, en miniature þÿ provided they could bv that means the sooner reach the goal of their wishes þÿ a heavy purse. Regardless, as the Diet has been, of the report of the Committee, still wo ought to be thankful for the Law as it is. It is a beginning ; and we hope to see it progress. This even appears to be intimated by the Committee, where it observes that þÿ it cannot hurt if forms of Legislation, in the beginning at least, until parliamentary tact is developed, be of such a kind as m»y þÿ prevent hasty measures

The constitution of one of the freest countries in the world, that of England, cannot be looked upon as the work of a day or a generation either, but has from time resembles, as þÿI aley to time been patched and altered to suit the age. sny3, one of those old mansions, þÿ It which, instead of being built all at once, after a regular plan, and according to the rules of architecture at present established, has been reared in different ages of the art, has been altered from time to time, and has been continually receiving additions and repairs, suited to the taste, fortune or conveniency of its successive proprietors. In such a building we look in vain for the elegance and proportion, for the just order and correspondence of parts which we expect in a modern edilice, and which external symmetry, after all, contribute much more perhaps to the amusement of the beholder than the accommodation of the inhabitant." Then again, let us bear in mind, that in all constitutions there exists a wide difference between the actual state of government and tbe theory. The most absolute powers, as in England, may be granted to the King, which may never be used, but dwindle into mere ceremonies. All therefore depends on the manner in which affairs are conducted ; lor the worst form of government, administered by men of knowledge, prudence and integrity, will secure the well-being ol' the people; whereas the best in the hands of folly and depravity, will bring on them numerous miseries.

In conclusion, I must call the attention of those who are invested w ith the high trust ol electing members to this Council. Let me advise them, in the execution of th.eir duty as electors, to divest themselves of all personal considerations. Vote lor no man, because he an acquaintance, a friend or an employer. Examine tbe public conduct and avowed sentiments of those for whom you would vote, and calmly consider whether they are such as you can approve of, or as being consistent with the general welfare of the people. Hear in mind, that if you act with levity and imprudence in appointing men, who, from their conduct and character, are unfitted to exercise tiie important function ot public representatives, you in more ways than one commit a crime against society, and are unworthy of possessing the valuable prerogatives with which you ato inv ested.
